content.poetic_cipher: The first distinction chooses no side.
content.cipher_explanation: The 'first distinction' represents the primitive XOR relation. 'Chooses no side' refers to commutativity: \(a \oplus b = b \oplus a\). XOR identifies difference without declaring which side of the difference is more real, primary, or privileged. The cipher therefore compresses the formal statement that distinction is relational rather than an ontological ranking of its operands.
content.handoff: A symmetric operation can be repeatedly applied. The mathematical result of allowing that operation to close over its domain is the Library.

sections.title: The Library as XOR Closure
sections.purpose: Characterize the Library as a static, maximally complete, unbounded relational totality satisfying XOR closure and self-containment, while explicitly separating mathematical closure from temporal, generative, or ontological construction.
sections.poetic_cypher: XOR is the distinction. The Library is the totality in which distinction is closed.
sections.cypher_explanation: XOR supplies the primitive operation of distinction. The Library is characterized by closure under that operation within the formal domain D, together with maximal completeness and self-containment with respect to the system's formal resources. Closure is a mathematical property of the Library, not a process by which the Library comes into existence. The observer subsequently appears as a derived relational structure whose accessibility and coherence are defined relative to the unchanged totality.

sections.title: Closure Under XOR
sections.purpose: Define the formal closure relation inherited from the primitive XOR operation while establishing that the Library itself is static, maximally complete, unbounded, and without a privileged exterior, origin, coordinate, or construction history.

content.text: The primitive operation \(\oplus\) does not by itself specify a physical ontology or a temporal process. It specifies an operation of distinction on a formal domain \(D\). Closure then provides the mathematical condition under which a collection of configurations remains closed under that operation. The resulting Library is not interpreted as something that is progressively generated by applying XOR. Rather, closure characterizes the structural completeness of a totality that is treated as already static and complete.

content.title: Definition 3.1 — Formal XOR Closure
content.text: Let \(D\) be the formal domain on which \(\oplus\) operates, and let \(G \subseteq D\) be a specified set of configurations used as mathematical generators for a representation. The XOR closure of \(G\) in \(D\), written \(\operatorname{Closure}_{D}(\oplus;G)\), is the smallest subset \(S \subseteq D\) such that \(G \subseteq S\) and, for every \(x,y \in S\), \(x \oplus y \in S\).

content.label: Formal closure characterization
content.latex: \operatorname{Closure}_{D}(\oplus;G) = \bigcap\left\{S \subseteq D \mid G \subseteq S \land \forall x,y \in S,\; x \oplus y \in S\right\}

content.text: The closure notation specifies a mathematical characterization. It does not imply that the elements of the closure are generated sequentially, that one configuration existed before another, or that a member of \(G\) constitutes an ontological first state. The generating set is representational: it supplies a description from which the closed structure may be mathematically specified, but it does not become an origin of the totality.

content.title: Definition 3.2 — Static Library
content.text: The Library \(\mathcal{M}\) is the maximally complete, unbounded totality satisfying XOR closure and self-containment with respect to the formal resources of the system. Closure describes a structural property of \(\mathcal{M}\); it is not a temporal, developmental, or ontological mechanism by which \(\mathcal{M}\) comes into existence.

The formal closure construction may be used to characterize an XOR-closed structure, but the semantic definition of the Library is stronger than closure minimality alone. The Library is treated as the complete static totality admitted by the formal ontology, not merely as a finite result produced by a particular generating history.

content.title: Definition 3.3 — Self-Containment
content.text: The Library is self-contained with respect to its formal resources: no configuration outside \(\mathcal{M}\) can function as a privileged exterior if that configuration is itself definable within the system using \(\oplus\), elements of \(\mathcal{M}\), and the formal domain \(D\).

content.label: No describable privileged exterior
content.latex: \neg\exists z \notin \mathcal{M}\;\text{such that }z\text{ is definable within the system using only }\oplus\text{ and elements of }\mathcal{M}\text{ over }D\text{ as a privileged exterior}

content.text: This condition does not assert that literal physical exteriority is independently impossible. It establishes a formal boundary condition: a privileged exterior that is describable using the same formal resources cannot remain external to the totality it is supposed to stand outside of. Any such candidate is already part of the formal relational structure under consideration.

content.title: Definition 3.4 — XOR Termination Singleton
content.text: The unique singleton termination class \(\mathcal{Z}\) is the subset of configurations satisfying self-cancellation as a fixed-point condition under XOR: \(\mathcal{Z} := \{z \in D \mid z \oplus z = z\}\). Under the Boolean XOR identities, this set is exactly \(\{0\}\).

For every \(x \in \mathcal{M}\), self-cancellation gives \(x \oplus x = 0\), and therefore \(x \oplus x \in \mathcal{Z}\). The singleton \(\mathcal{Z}\) is consequently internal to the Library whenever \(0 \in \mathcal{M}\), as follows from XOR closure together with the presence of any configuration in \(\mathcal{M}\). It is not an exterior, boundary, edge, or region beyond the Library.

The identity element also satisfies \(0 \oplus x = x\). Thus \(0\) is not a point outside the relational structure but its internal XOR identity. When the recursive bounce relation \((x \oplus y) \oplus y = x\) is evaluated at \(y=0\), it reduces immediately to \((x \oplus 0) \oplus 0 = x\). The distinction has therefore reached the identity state in which the second application introduces no new change.

The relation \(x \sim y \iff x \oplus y = 0\) defines equality for Boolean XOR, since \(x \oplus y = 0\) holds exactly when \(x=y\). Consequently, each configuration forms its own equivalence class, and \(\mathcal{Z}=\{0\}\) is specifically the singleton equivalence class containing the XOR identity.

𝒵 is therefore complementary to the non-degenerate relational structure in a structural sense: it represents completed self-cancellation or termination of distinction rather than an exterior to distinction. The complement \(\mathcal{M} \setminus \mathcal{Z}\) contains configurations that are not the XOR identity, while \(\mathcal{Z}\) contains the completed identity state. This is termination versus non-degenerate distinction, not inside versus outside.

content.title: Definition 3.5 — Reference-Frame Neutrality
content.text: No configuration in \(\mathcal{M}\) is privileged as the ontological origin of the Library. Any admissible configuration \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) may serve as an observer-relative reference configuration without becoming a privileged origin or changing the Library itself.

content.label: Arbitrary reference invariance
content.latex: \forall x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\quad x\text{ may serve as a relational reference without altering }\mathcal{M}

content.text: The choice of \(G\) does not weaken this neutrality. A mathematical generating description may be useful for specifying the closure, but no member of \(G\) acquires ontological priority merely because it was selected as a generator. Treating a generator as a privileged physical beginning would convert a representational choice into an additional axiom.

content.title: Definition 3.6 — Static Maximality
content.text: The Library is interpreted as maximally complete relative to the formal ontology of the model. No configuration admitted by that ontology is excluded merely because it has not been encountered by an observer, lies outside an observer's current coherent continuation, or was not included in a particular traversal history.

The index \(i\) in this expression is merely a formal notation for invariance and does not denote successive temporal copies of the Library. The Library does not expand, contract, become more complete, or become more complex as an observer traverses it. Changes in apparent succession or complexity belong to the observer's changing relation to the unchanged totality.

Static maximality must not be confused with closure minimality. The closure construction identifies the smallest XOR-closed subset containing a chosen generating set. The semantic interpretation of \(\mathcal{M}\) as the maximally complete totality is an additional definitional condition of this axiomatic floor. It is not claimed that maximality follows mathematically from closure minimality alone.

content.title: Definition 3.7 — Whole-Library Relationality
content.text: An observer-relative reference configuration is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library rather than occupying an ontologically isolated local portion of it. Observer state, history, resolution, and coherence determine accessible relations; they do not determine membership in \(\mathcal{M}\).

content.label: Accessibility as a relation over the Library

content.text: A configuration can therefore remain a member of \(\mathcal{M}\) even when it is inaccessible, indistinguishable, or incoherent relative to a particular observer. Accessibility is a relation over the Library rather than a mechanism for creating or deleting Library membership.

The same separation applies to 𝒵. Reaching the termination singleton does not erase a configuration from the Library. Rather, self-cancellation maps the configuration's XOR relation to the internal identity state \(0\). Termination is therefore a relational property of the operation, not an ontological boundary of the totality.

At the axiomatic floor, membership in \(\mathcal{M}\) carries no implication of persistence, coherence, observability, accessibility, physical realization, consciousness, or causal participation. Those properties belong to later relational constructions defined over the unchanged Library.

The central distinction is therefore between closure and generation. Closure states that the Library is structurally invariant under XOR. It does not describe a universe being assembled one XOR operation at a time. Likewise, observer traversal does not cause configurations to become members of the Library. The observer's relation changes; \(\mathcal{M}\) does not.
Closure draws no road through time; it names the totality in which every relational road already belongs.

XOR supplies distinction. Closure supplies the mathematical condition that keeps distinction internal to the closed structure. The Library is then defined as the static, maximally complete, unbounded totality satisfying that closure condition and self-containment. 𝒵 is the internal identity state reached by self-cancellation, not an exterior or boundary. No generator, configuration, worldline, coordinate, or observer is privileged as the ontological origin of the totality.

With XOR closure, static maximality, self-containment, and the internal termination singleton established, the next subsection examines the relational character of the Library itself. Section 3.2 therefore distinguishes the complete static totality from any observer-accessible subset, answer-space interpretation, local neighborhood, or generated future.

content.opening: The Library is best understood at this stage not as a physical place, an answer space, or a region through which an observer progressively searches, but as the static, maximally complete total configuration domain of the NSFG construction. It is a dimensionally undifferentiated relational totality characterized by closure under the primitive operation \(\oplus\), together with self-containment and the absence of a privileged definable exterior. Closure specifies a mathematical property of the Library; it does not describe a chronological, developmental, or ontological process by which the Library is generated. The Library therefore does not begin in a simple state and become more complex. It is maximally complete at every abstract traversal index. Formally, \(\forall i,\; \mathcal{M}_i = \mathcal{M}\). Apparent succession, increasing complexity, locality, distance, and restriction of possible continuations arise from the observer's changing relation to this unchanged totality.

static_totality.definition: The Library is the static, maximally complete, unbounded relational totality satisfying closure under the primitive distinction operation \(\oplus\), self-containment with respect to the formal resources of the system, and absence of a privileged definable exterior. It is not a physical container, metric space, temporal sequence, generated structure, or singularity.
static_totality.closure_qualification: The closure condition specifies a mathematical property of \(\mathcal{M}\). It does not imply that \(\mathcal{M}\) came into existence through successive applications of \(\oplus\), nor does it introduce a temporal or ontological generation process.
static_totality.self_containment: \(\mathcal{M}\) contains no privileged exterior configuration definable within the system using only the primitive operation \(\oplus\) and elements of \(\mathcal{M}\) over the formal domain \(D\).
static_totality.interpretation: Any notation suggesting a sequence of Library states is therefore a representational device for describing observer traversal or changing relational reference. It does not represent distinct temporal versions of the Library being created, destroyed, or modified.

unboundedness.definition: Unboundedness means that the axiomatic floor imposes no privileged finite boundary, terminal region, coordinate limit, or externally supplied truncation on \(\mathcal{M}\). It does not require a particular cardinality, dimensionality, metric, or physical interpretation.
unboundedness.formal_statement: No axiom of the axiomatic floor imposes a privileged finite cardinality, finite dimensionality, metric boundary, terminal coordinate, or excluded region on \(\mathcal{M}\).
unboundedness.interpretation: The Library has no intrinsic edge at which coherent traversal must terminate merely because of a configuration's location within the totality. Unboundedness therefore describes the absence of an imposed boundary condition rather than a claim that every conceivable mathematical object is necessarily represented.
unboundedness.reference_neutrality: Because no coordinate, region, or configuration is privileged as the boundary of \(\mathcal{M}\), any admissible \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) may serve as an observer-relative reference without becoming an ontological origin or boundary.

maximal_completeness.definition: The Library is maximally complete because no configuration, construction history, reference configuration, coordinate, or worldline is privileged as the universal origin from which the whole must be generated or ordered.
maximal_completeness.reference_neutrality: Any admissible configuration \(x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}}\) may serve as an observer-relative reference without changing the Library itself.
maximal_completeness.structural_requirement: If coherent traversal were fundamentally available only from configurations associated with a privileged construction origin, that origin would constitute a hidden privileged worldline or reference frame. The maximal Library formulation removes this asymmetry by requiring the underlying totality to remain unchanged when the observer-relative reference is changed.
maximal_completeness.continuation_consequence: The requirement that every admissible reference configuration admit at least one coherent continuation is a derived structural requirement of the combined NSFG assumptions. It is not claimed to follow from XOR closure or maximality alone.
maximal_completeness.qualification: The nonempty-continuation condition applies only where the observer state itself admits continuation. It is a requirement on the observer-relative traversal structure, not a claim that every configuration in \(\mathcal{M}\) is automatically coherent, observable, or traversable by every observer.

membership.definition: A configuration belongs to the Library by virtue of membership in the complete total configuration domain, not because it is an answer, a coherent continuation, an observable state, or an accessible state.
membership.formal_statement: \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) means that \(x\) belongs to the formally defined total configuration domain.
membership.important_distinction: Membership is distinct from persistence, distinguishability, coherence, accessibility, observability, physical interpretation, and usefulness to an observer.
membership.non_filtering_principle: \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) does not imply that \(x\) is persistent, coherent, physical, observable, or accessible to any observer.
membership.non_erasure_principle: \(x \notin A_O\) does not imply \(x \notin \mathcal{M}\). Failure of observer-relative accessibility, coherence, or distinguishability does not remove a configuration from the totality.

unfiltered_totality.explanation: The Library is unfiltered at the axiomatic level. No observer-relative resolution threshold, persistence condition, coherence criterion, accessibility relation, or physical interpretation is applied to determine Library membership. These structures arise only as relations over the already complete totality.
unfiltered_totality.formal_statement: \(\mathcal{M}\) contains configurations independently of whether those configurations participate in an observer-relative coherent traversal.
unfiltered_totality.consequence: Coherent and incoherent configurations therefore belong to the same underlying total configuration domain. Coherence does not divide the Library into ontologically real and unreal regions. Instead, coherence specifies which relations and paths can be maintained relative to an observer, its history, its current reference configuration, and its resolution.
unfiltered_totality.observer_relation: The observer does not search inside a pre-filtered answer space. The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library and induces an observer-relative structure over \(\mathcal{M}\).

whole_library_relationality.definition: The Library supplies the whole relational domain over which observer-relative paths, coherence, accessibility, distinguishability, and continuation are evaluated.
whole_library_relationality.coherence_relation: \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x)\) evaluates a path \(\gamma\) relative to observer \(O\), relevant history \(h\), and current reference configuration \(x\).
whole_library_relationality.reference_neutrality: Changing the observer's current reference configuration \(x\) changes the observer-relative relational evaluation without changing \(\mathcal{M}\).
whole_library_relationality.whole_library_relation: The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library at every abstract traversal step. The observer does not first receive a locally bounded subset of \(\mathcal{M}\) and then search inside that subset.
whole_library_relationality.occupancy_clarification: The observer's worldline is represented as an observer-relative relational structure over the totality. Its experienced traversal is nevertheless restricted to the coherent continuations maintained from its current reference, history, and resolution.
whole_library_relationality.adjacency_clarification: At the axiomatic floor, relational availability does not imply intrinsic spatial adjacency. The Library has no primitive metric distance or dimensional coordinate system. Any experienced notion of near, far, local, or remote belongs to a later observer-relative structure.

relational_structure.definition: The Library may be represented relationally as a maximally connected configuration domain in which configurations can stand in formal relation without requiring intrinsic spatial separation.
relational_structure.dimensionality: \(\mathcal{M}\) has no intrinsic dimensionality at the axiomatic floor.
relational_structure.metric: No metric or distance function is primitive to \(\mathcal{M}\).
relational_structure.separation: Any experienced separation between configurations is observer-relative and belongs to a derived relational structure rather than to the foundational ontology.
relational_structure.movement: Traversal is not spatial movement through a pre-existing metric space. It is the ordered maintenance or selection of coherent relations among configurations already contained in \(\mathcal{M}\).
relational_structure.complete_graph_analogy: A complete graph is a useful mathematical analogy for expressing the absence of intrinsically isolated configurations: every configuration may participate in a relation with every other configuration without requiring geometric distance. This analogy is representational only and does not introduce graph topology as an additional physical axiom.

answer_space_interpretation.explanation: The term 'answer space' may still be used for an observer-relative subset of configurations or continuations satisfying a particular query, coherence relation, or navigation criterion. It must not, however, be used as the ontological definition of \(\mathcal{M}\). The Library is prior to any particular question.
answer_space_interpretation.formal_distinction: \(\mathcal{M}\) is the complete total configuration domain, while an observer-relative answer or continuation space is a derived structure over \(\mathcal{M}\).
answer_space_interpretation.consequence: The observer does not determine what exists by filtering the Library. It determines which relations within the unchanged totality are distinguishable, coherent, accessible, or relevant from a particular relational reference.

observer_effect.explanation: Because the Library itself is invariant, apparent development must be attributed to the observer's changing traversal relation rather than to ontological growth or modification of the totality.
observer_effect.interpretation: What appears to the observer as progression from simple to complex is therefore a change in the observer's relational position and maintained distinctions within an unchanged maximally complete totality. The Library itself does not become more complex.
observer_effect.emergent_structure: Apparent temporal sequence, locality, distance, complexity, and restriction of possible continuation are therefore candidates for later observer-relative derived structures rather than axioms of the Library itself.

content.poetic_cipher: The Library is not the answers. It is the whole relation in which answers can become paths.
content.cipher_explanation: The Library contains configurations without classifying them as answers, futures, coherent states, observable states, or accessible states. Those classifications arise only through observer-relative relations over the totality. A path is therefore not a thing generated by the Library; it is an observer-relative coherent ordering among configurations already contained within \(\mathcal{M}\). The totality does not change when the observer changes its relation to it.
formal_summary: \(\forall x,y \in \mathcal{M},\; x \oplus y \in \mathcal{M}\) specifies the Library's closure property.
Closure is a mathematical property of \(\mathcal{M}\) and does not represent temporal, developmental, or ontological generation.
\(\forall i,\; \mathcal{M}_i = \mathcal{M}\): the Library is static and maximally complete at every abstract traversal index.
\(\mathcal{M}\) has no privileged intrinsic origin, coordinate, worldline, metric boundary, or observer reference.
Any admissible \(x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}}\) may serve as an observer-relative reference without altering \(\mathcal{M}\).
\(x \in \mathcal{M}\) does not imply persistence, distinguishability, coherence, physicality, observability, or accessibility.
Observer-relative answer spaces and coherent continuation spaces are derived structures over \(\mathcal{M}\), not replacements for \(\mathcal{M}\).
The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library rather than ontologically localized to a temporally generated neighborhood.
The Library has no intrinsic dimensionality or metric distance at the axiomatic floor.
Apparent temporal or complexity growth belongs to observer traversal and does not represent evolution of the Library.
The requirement \(\forall x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\; \Gamma_O(h,x) \neq \varnothing\) is a derived structural requirement and is not asserted to follow from XOR closure alone.
content.handoff: If the Library is a static, maximally complete total configuration domain rather than an observer-generated answer space, the next question is whether any configuration that can be meaningfully described as external can remain outside that totality without introducing a privileged relation beyond the axiomatic floor.

sections.title: No Exterior, No Privileged Perspective
sections.purpose: Derive the absence of a privileged God's-eye perspective from the closure construction without introducing an additional physical or observational axiom.
sections.poetic_cypher: There is no balcony outside the Library from which the Library can be judged.
sections.cypher_explanation: The Library is defined as the XOR closure of the formal domain D. A perspective that can be described within the same formal machinery is itself representable within D and therefore cannot remain ontologically external to the closure. The metaphor of the balcony denotes a supposedly privileged external standpoint; the formal result is that such a describable standpoint cannot be both external to \(\mathcal{M}\) and represented by the same formal system.

subsections.title: The Exterior Problem
subsections.purpose: Examine whether a configuration or perspective can function as a privileged reference outside the Library, and distinguish the formal impossibility of a privileged external relation from the broader philosophical question of whether something might exist beyond the theory's defined vocabulary.

content.opening: The static-totality interpretation raises a precise reference problem: can there be a privileged perspective from which the Library as a whole is resolved, ordered, or judged while that perspective itself remains external to the relational structure being described? At this stage, an exterior is not defined geometrically or physically. It is defined formally as a proposed configuration or perspective that is both relevant to the description of the Library and claimed to stand outside the Library's relational domain.

definition.text: Let \(\mathcal{M}\) denote the Library. The Library is formally characterized through the closure relation \(\mathcal{M} := \operatorname{Closure}_{D}(\oplus)\), but this closure is not interpreted as a temporal generation process. An external candidate is a proposed configuration or perspective \(\Omega\) satisfying \(\Omega \notin \mathcal{M}\) while simultaneously being invoked as a reference for resolving relations within \(\mathcal{M}\).
mathematics: \(\Omega \text{ is invoked as a reference for relations within } \mathcal{M}\)

argument.statement: Suppose \(\Omega\) is proposed as an external reference capable of resolving or judging the Library as a whole.

If \(\Omega\) is represented as a configuration using the same formal machinery that defines the axiomatic domain, then that representation is part of the formal configuration domain to which the closure construction applies.
If the represented configuration \(\Omega\) is admitted by the primitive operation and is reachable under the closure relation, then the closure places it within the Library.
The proposed configuration can therefore not simultaneously be an internally represented XOR-generable configuration and remain outside the Library.

The important consequence is not that every conceivable exterior is metaphysically impossible, but that an internally represented configuration cannot acquire privileged external status merely by being declared external.
argument.formal_form: \(\Omega \text{ internally represented and XOR-generable} \Rightarrow \Omega \notin \text{a privileged external class}\)

reference_problem.text: The deeper issue is relational rather than merely set-theoretic. A perspective does not become a privileged reference frame simply because it is postulated outside the Library. To resolve distinctions within \(\mathcal{M}\), an external perspective would require a specified relation connecting it to the configurations being resolved. If that relation is not part of the formal system, the perspective contributes no additional internal coherence rule. If the relation is introduced into the formal system, then the relation itself becomes part of the described structure and must be accounted for by the same ontology.
mathematics: \(R_{\Omega} \in \text{axiomatic vocabulary} \Rightarrow \text{the relation is part of the described formal structure}\)

important_distinction.text: This result must not be confused with the claim that nothing can exist beyond the Library in every imaginable philosophical or mathematical sense. The axiomatic floor makes a narrower claim. An object or perspective that is completely undefined within the formal system is simply outside the theory's vocabulary, and no conclusion about its existence is derived. An object or perspective that is represented within the formal machinery, however, cannot be granted a special ontological status merely by labeling it external.

undefined_or_unknowable.description: A proposed object may have no representation within the formal system. In that case, the axiomatic floor makes no derivation concerning its existence, structure, or relation to the Library.
undefined_or_unknowable.formal_status: \(\Omega \text{ undefined in the formal system} \Rightarrow \text{no derivation about } \Omega\)

describable_exterior.description: A proposed exterior that is represented as a configuration using the same formal machinery is no longer available as an unexplained privileged reference. If that configuration is admitted to the XOR-generable domain, it belongs to the Library under the closure characterization.

external_reference_without_relation.description: A perspective may be verbally postulated as external without thereby acquiring a coherence relation to the Library. Without an internally specified relation, it supplies no God's-eye resolver for distinctions within the Library.

content.scope_note: The conclusion is deliberately weaker than a claim that nothing can exist beyond the Library in every imaginable philosophical or mathematical sense. The axiomatic result concerns the availability of a privileged external reference relation. Such a relation cannot be assumed merely by postulating an exterior. It must either remain undefined, in which case the axiomatic floor derives nothing from it, or be represented within the formal structure, in which case it loses its status as an unexplained privileged standpoint.
content.derived_result: A describable XOR-generable configuration cannot remain an unexplained privileged exterior to \(\mathcal{M}\), and an undefined exterior supplies no derived coherence relation to \(\mathcal{M}\). Therefore the axiomatic floor provides no privileged external God's-eye resolver. Reference must instead be established relationally within the formal structure.

handoff_logic.premise: No privileged external coherence relation is supplied by the axiomatic floor.
handoff_logic.consequence: No observer may be assigned an absolute God's-eye resolution rule merely by being declared external or universal.
handoff_logic.next_construction: Observerhood can therefore be introduced structurally as a persistent configuration with observer-relative resolution, while preserving the Library as a single static totality.

mathematics.undefined_relation: \(R_{\Omega} \text{ not specified} \Rightarrow \text{no derived privileged coherence relation}\)
mathematics.internalized_relation: \(R_{\Omega} \text{ specified within the formal system} \Rightarrow R_{\Omega} \text{ is part of the described structure}\)
mathematics.conclusion: \(\text{no privileged external reference relation is derivable from the axiomatic floor}\)

subsections.poetic_cypher: There is no balcony outside the Library from which the Library can be judged.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The balcony represents a supposedly privileged standpoint that is both relevant to the Library and external to it. Merely naming such a standpoint does not provide it with a coherence relation. If it remains undefined, the axiomatic floor derives nothing from it. If it is represented as an XOR-generable configuration, it belongs to the Library under the closure characterization. The cipher therefore compresses the distinction between an imagined exterior and a privileged external reference: the former may be postulated without consequence, while the latter requires an additional relation that cannot be smuggled in as a God's-eye rule.
subsections.handoff: Without a privileged exterior supplying an absolute resolution rule, observer resolution must be treated as relational rather than universal. The next construction can therefore define observerhood structurally from persistent distinguishability, while keeping the observer relationally situated with respect to the unchanged totality \(\mathcal{M}\).

subsections.title: No God's-Eye Resolver
subsections.poetic_cipher: The Library has no master lens.
subsections.content: A privileged resolver would be a hypothetical observer-independent rule that determines, for every pair of configurations, whether their distinction is universally resolved. Formally, let U : D × D → {0,1}, where U(x,y)=1 means that the distinction between x and y is resolved by the rule, and U(x,y)=0 means that it is not. Such a rule would assign a single resolution outcome to every pair independently of any observer configuration. The axiomatic floor does not contain such a rule. The sole primitive operation is XOR, defined on the formal domain D. XOR determines whether two operands differ within the Boolean operation itself: a ⊕ b = 1 if and only if a ≠ b. It does not determine whether that distinction is resolvable by an observer, whether the distinction persists, or whether it should count as accessible. Those are additional relations that require additional structure. Therefore U is not derivable merely from the existence and algebraic properties of XOR. In the notation of the axiomatic floor, U ∉ A_N unless U is explicitly introduced as an additional axiom. Introducing U would change the foundational system by supplying a universal resolution predicate that was not present in the original primitive. This distinction is important. XOR establishes difference; it does not establish a universal scale on which every difference must be resolved. A pair of configurations may therefore be distinct under the formal operation while remaining indistinguishable to a particular observer. The absence of U leaves room for resolution to be relational rather than absolute. Accordingly, NSFG permits an observer-relative resolution relation. For an observer O, a later construction may define a relation D_O(x,y) according to O's own resolution capacity. This does not mean that O creates the distinction between x and y. The distinction already exists within the formal configuration domain. Rather, O determines which distinctions remain effectively resolvable relative to its own structural resolution floor. The consequence is not that every observer has an arbitrary private reality. Rather, the axiomatic floor refuses to privilege one resolution rule as universally authoritative. Observer-relative resolution can therefore be introduced without contradicting XOR, provided that the observer and its resolution capacity are themselves defined as downstream structures rather than smuggled into the primitive. The Library consequently has no master lens: there is no axiom at the floor that selects, from outside all observers, which distinctions must count as universally resolved. Any such lens would be additional structure, not a consequence of XOR. The ability to resolve a distinction must therefore belong to the structure doing the resolving. This provides the formal handoff to the subsequent definition of observer-relative distinguishability and the threshold I_N(O).

mathematics.resolution_interpretation: U(x,y)=1 means that the distinction between x and y is universally resolved; U(x,y)=0 means that it is not.
mathematics.axiomatic_status: U \notin A_N unless explicitly introduced as an additional axiom.
mathematics.consequence: XOR determines formal distinction but does not supply an observer-independent resolution predicate.
mathematics.observer_relative_relation: D_O(x,y) may be introduced as an observer-relative resolution relation derived from the resolution capacity of O.
mathematics.threshold_handoff: I_N(O) is introduced downstream as the observer-relative resolution floor.

formal_claims: U is not part of the stated axiomatic floor.
U cannot be treated as a consequence of XOR merely because XOR determines whether operands differ.
Adding U would constitute the introduction of a new axiom or equivalent additional structure.
The axiomatic floor therefore does not contain an observer-independent resolution predicate.
Observer-relative resolution does not imply that observers create distinctions or that inaccessible configurations cease to exist.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The master lens represents a hypothetical universal resolution rule U. The absence of such a lens means that no single observer-independent mechanism is authorized to decide which distinctions are resolved everywhere. XOR supplies distinction itself, but not the resolution capacity with which that distinction is evaluated. The lens therefore belongs, if introduced at all, to the resolving structure rather than to the primitive operation.
subsections.handoff: If there is no universal lens, the ability to resolve a distinction must belong to the structure doing the resolving. The next construction therefore defines observer-relative distinguishability and the observer-specific resolution threshold I_N(O).

derived: The Library is closed under the primitive operation by definition.
A describable external candidate represented within the same formal machinery belongs to the formal domain.
An XOR-generable candidate belongs to the Library by closure.
A describable XOR-generable candidate therefore cannot remain external to the Library.
The axiomatic floor does not provide a privileged God's-eye configuration.
not_derived: The nonexistence of every conceivable metaphysical exterior.
The nonexistence of unknowable or undefined entities.
The physical structure of the universe.
The existence or nature of consciousness.
The existence of any particular observer.
A physical interpretation of the Library.

invariants_preserved: The Library remains a definition rather than an additional axiom.
Closure is explicitly taken over the domain D.
Inaccessibility is not treated as erasure.
The Library is not treated as a physical container.
The distinction between formal non-membership and unknowability is preserved.
The conclusion is restricted to describable privileged exteriors.

sections.title: Observer-Relative Resolution
sections.purpose: Introduce the observer and its resolution capacity without making either primitive.
sections.poetic_cipher: The observer is a difference that remains. The boundary of its remaining is its resolution.
sections.cypher_explanation: The first sentence identifies observerhood with persistence of distinguishability rather than with consciousness or intention. The second identifies resolution as the boundary determining which distinctions can remain stably distinguishable for that observer. The formal resolution threshold is introduced only after observerhood has been established structurally.
sections.introduction: The axiomatic floor has so far defined distinction and the closure generated by distinction, but it has not yet specified what it means for a configuration to maintain a distinction. This section introduces the observer without treating observation as a primitive act. An observer is instead derived as a configuration whose structure permits distinctions to persist across successive states. The observer therefore belongs to the Library in the same formal sense as every other configuration. What distinguishes it is not consciousness, intention, or privileged status, but persistence. Once such a structure is identified, a further question becomes unavoidable: which distinctions can that structure actually maintain? This motivates observer-relative resolution.
sections.scope_boundary: At this stage, observerhood is a structural property only. No claim is made that an observer is conscious, biological, intelligent, physical, or capable of intentional measurement. Those interpretations, if introduced later, are downstream of the axiomatic construction.

subsections.title: Observer as a Derived Structure
subsections.purpose: Define observerhood structurally rather than psychologically, establish observer membership in the Library, and defer consciousness and other interpretive properties to downstream theory.
subsections.content:
An observer is not introduced as a new primitive entity. Since the Library is already defined as the XOR closure of the formal domain, any observer must itself be a configuration within that closure. Observerhood is therefore a property of a configuration, not a separate ontological category. Let \(O\) denote a configuration in the Library. We call \(O\) an observer when its structure is capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions across successive states. The word persistent is important: a single distinction does not constitute an observer. Observerhood requires a continuing structure in which distinctions remain available rather than immediately collapsing into indistinguishability. Formally, observerhood is written as: \[
O \in \mathcal{M}
\] and: \[
O \text{ is an observer} \iff O \text{ is a configuration in } \mathcal{M} \text{ containing a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.}
\] The term resolvable is deliberately structural rather than psychological. It does not mean that \(O\) consciously notices, interprets, or understands a distinction. It means only that the distinction can remain sufficiently differentiated within the structure represented by \(O\). The quantitative boundary governing that distinction has not yet been introduced; it will be defined through the observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\) in the following subsection. This distinction prevents observerhood from being smuggled into the axiomatic floor as consciousness. A configuration may satisfy the structural definition of observerhood without possessing any assumed mental state. Consciousness is therefore not required at the axiomatic level. Whether some later physical or cognitive systems instantiate additional properties associated with conscious observation is a separate question and cannot be inferred from the definition alone. The observer is consequently derived from the same ontology as everything else. It is not outside the Library, above the Library, or granted a privileged position within it. It is a configuration whose internal persistence permits distinctions to remain available across a continuing chain. The dependency is therefore: \[
\text{distinction} \;\rightarrow\; \text{persistence} \;\rightarrow\; \text{observerhood}.
\] The construction has not yet supplied a universal rule determining how much distinction is required for persistence. That question belongs to the observer itself. To say that a distinction survives requires a boundary separating distinctions that remain effective from distinctions that fall below the observer's effective resolution.

mathematics.observer_definition: O \text{ is an observer} \iff O \text{ is a configuration in } \mathcal{M} \text{ that contains a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.}

subsections.formal_status: The membership condition and structural definition are formal constructions from the stated ontology. The absence of a consciousness requirement is a scope constraint on the axiomatic system, not a claim that consciousness is impossible or irrelevant in downstream theories.
subsections.poetic_cypher: An observer is a difference that survives long enough to have another difference.
subsections.cypher_explanation: A difference represents a distinction. Surviving represents persistence across successive states. Having another difference represents the continuation of distinguishable structure. The cipher therefore compresses observerhood as a persistent structure without introducing consciousness, intention, or any privileged observer.
subsections.handoff: To say that a distinction survives, we must specify the boundary at which a distinction remains effective for the structure that carries it. That boundary is observer-relative resolution, represented by \(I_N(O)\).

content.opening: Once observerhood has been defined as a persistent capacity to maintain distinctions, the next question is not whether distinctions exist in the Library, but which distinctions a particular observer can maintain as stable distinctions. This requires a resolution threshold. The Noor-Planck threshold, written I_N(O), is introduced here as an observer-relative structural quantity. It does not describe a limit imposed by the Library itself, nor does it determine which configurations belong to the Library. It describes the minimum effective distinction that observer O can preserve as a stable distinction within its own configuration.

subsections.title: The Threshold Belongs to the Observer
subsections.content: Let Obs denote the class of configurations that satisfy the structural definition of observerhood. Define the resolution-threshold function as
mathematics: I_N(O) = \text{the minimum effective distinction magnitude that observer } O \text{ can maintain as a stable distinction}.
subsections.explanation: The important point is the placement of the argument O. The threshold is not introduced as a universal constant I_N. It is written I_N(O), because the resolution floor belongs to the observer configuration being considered. Two observers may therefore occupy the same Library while maintaining different effective resolutions. This difference concerns their respective capacities to maintain distinctions; it does not imply that the underlying Library differs between them.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The ruler belongs to the hand that can hold it.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The ruler represents the observer's resolution threshold. The hand represents the observer as a structural configuration. The metaphor does not imply subjective choice: the threshold is a property of the observer's capacity to maintain distinctions.

subsections.title: I_N(O) Is Not a Property of the Library
subsections.content: The Library is a static totality characterized formally through the closure of the formal domain under XOR. This closure notation specifies the mathematical structure of the Library; it does not describe a temporal process by which the Library is progressively generated. Library membership is therefore independent of whether a particular observer can distinguish or maintain a given distinction. Nothing in the axiomatic floor supplies a universal minimum distinction magnitude for the totality itself.
mathematics: I_N(O) \text{ is observer-indexed and is not defined as a universal resolution constant of } \mathcal{M}.
subsections.explanation: A distinction may therefore exist within \mathcal{M} without being stably resolvable by O. If observer O cannot maintain a distinction because its magnitude lies below I_N(O), that limitation changes the observer's effective description of the relation. It does not remove either configuration from the Library, alter Library membership, or collapse the underlying totality. The observer's resolution floor changes what can be maintained as a distinction, not what exists in \mathcal{M}.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The eye closes before the Library does.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Loss of distinction is a property of the observer's resolution, not deletion from the totality. The Library remains unchanged even when a distinction falls below the observer's effective resolution.

subsections.title: Observer Variability
subsections.content: Because the threshold is indexed to observer structure, different observers may have different resolution floors. The axiomatic floor permits this variability rather than imposing equality between observers.
mathematics: \exists O_1,O_2 \in \mathrm{Obs} \text{ such that } I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2) \text{ is permitted.}
subsections.explanation: This does not mean that every arbitrary threshold assignment is valid. Each I_N(O) is intended to characterize the structural capacity of the corresponding observer to maintain distinctions. The threshold is therefore observer-relative without being a freely chosen parameter. Two observers can relate to the same unchanged Library while maintaining different effective resolutions of that Library.
subsections.poetic_cypher: Two hands may hold different rulers, yet each ruler still has a length.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Different observers may have different resolution floors, but each threshold remains a definite structural quantity for the observer to which it belongs. Observer relativity therefore does not imply arbitrariness.

subsections.title: No Universal Threshold Is Assumed
subsections.content: The axiomatic floor does not assert the existence of a single threshold shared by every observer. Nor does it require the negation of such a universal value. The present construction simply leaves universality unestablished unless it is derived from additional structure.
mathematics: \forall O \in \mathrm{Obs},\ I_N(O) = I_N^* \text{ is not an axiom of the present construction.}
\exists I_N^*\ \forall O \in \mathrm{Obs},\ I_N(O) = I_N^* \text{ may be investigated only as a derived or additional result.}
subsections.explanation: This distinction preserves the logical scope of the axiomatic floor. A universal threshold and an observer-relative threshold make different commitments, but the absence of a universal axiom is not itself a proof that no universal value could ever emerge. A later theory may derive a common scale, identify conditions under which observer thresholds converge, or demonstrate that they remain distinct. None of those possibilities is assumed here.
subsections.poetic_cypher: One floor is not built into the whole Library; each structure stands on its own threshold.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The present axioms assign the resolution floor to the observer rather than to the Library as a universal law. Whether a deeper derivation produces a common scale remains an open downstream question.

subsections.title: Relative Does Not Mean Arbitrary
subsections.content: Calling I_N(O) observer-relative does not make distinguishability a matter of arbitrary preference. The observer is itself a configuration in the Library, and its threshold is intended to be determined by the structural capacity of that configuration to maintain distinctions. Thus the threshold is relative to a particular observer while remaining constrained by the structure of that observer.
mathematics: I_N(O) = \text{the structural resolution floor associated with the distinction-maintenance capacity of } O.
subsections.explanation: The distinction is therefore between relativity and arbitrariness. Relative means that the value is indexed to the observer under consideration. Arbitrary would mean that the value could be assigned without regard to the observer's structure. The axiomatic construction requires the former and does not imply the latter. The threshold belongs to the observer-relative relation between a configuration and the distinctions that configuration can maintain; it does not become a new ontological boundary inside the Library.
subsections.poetic_cypher: The measure follows the measurer, not the world.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The observer's resolution determines the distinctions that can be maintained by that observer. It does not determine the contents, membership, or completeness of the Library.

content.formal_conclusion: The introduction of I_N(O) establishes an observer-relative resolution condition without making resolution an ontological filter on the Library. The static totality \mathcal{M} remains unchanged regardless of the resolution of a particular observer. A distinction may therefore belong to \mathcal{M} while remaining below the effective resolution of O. Different observers may possess different resolution floors, and no universal value of I_N is assumed at the axiomatic level. The resulting separation is foundational: Library membership concerns what belongs to \mathcal{M}; observer-relative resolution concerns what O can maintain as a distinction. The next construction can therefore distinguish ontological membership from observer-relative distinguishability, accessibility, and ultimately coherence without allowing any of those relations to shrink or redefine the totality.
content.handoff: With the observer-specific resolution floor established independently of Library membership, the next section can formalize the difference between a distinction that exists within \mathcal{M} and a distinction that observer O can resolve and maintain.
content.poetic_cypher: The eye closes before the Library does.
content.cypher_explanation: The resolution threshold belongs to the observer's capacity rather than to the Library as a universal law. What falls below the observer's resolution is not erased from the totality; it simply ceases to function as a maintained distinction for that observer.

sections.title: Persistence and the Birth of the Observer
sections.purpose: Formalize survivable distinctions and derive observerhood as persistent structure.
sections.poetic_cypher: A distinction that can be kept is a distinction that can persist. A structure that persists its distinctions becomes an observer.
sections.cypher_explanation: The section moves from the observer-relative resolution relation established in the preceding definitions toward observerhood as a derived structural property. No consciousness, intention, agency, or human perception is required. An observer is introduced only as a configuration capable of maintaining distinctions that remain resolvable above its own threshold I_N(O) across a sequence of transitions.

subsections.title: Distinguishability Relative to O
subsections.purpose: Define observer-relative distinguishability while explicitly separating resolution from ontological membership in the static Library. This section establishes that an observer may collapse distinctions operationally without collapsing configurations ontologically, and that observer-relative accessibility is a relation imposed over the unchanged totality rather than a restriction on Library membership.
subsections.poetic_cypher: Two shadows may merge without the things casting them becoming one.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Observer resolution may cause distinct configurations to occupy the same effective resolution class for a particular observer. This operational identification does not alter the configurations themselves, does not identify them within the Library, and does not remove either configuration from the static totality. Resolution therefore changes the observer-relative description of the Library rather than the Library's membership.

content.opening: The Library is a static totality whose membership is not determined by any particular observer's resolution. Every configuration considered in this section is already a member of \(\mathcal{M}\); the question is not whether the observer causes that configuration to exist, but whether the observer can maintain a distinction between configurations at its available resolution. Once an observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\) has been introduced, distinguishability becomes relational: the same pair of configurations may constitute a stable distinction for one observer while falling below the resolution threshold of another. This difference belongs to the observer-relative relation, not to the ontological status of the configurations.
content.definition_distinguishability_magnitude: Let \(O\) be an observer and let \(x,y \in \mathcal{M}\). Define the observer-relative distinguishability magnitude by \(\delta_O(x,y) \geq 0\). The quantity \(\delta_O(x,y)\) represents the effective magnitude of the distinction between \(x\) and \(y\) as resolved by \(O\). It is therefore a relational quantity: it characterizes how the distinction is available to \(O\), not an observer-independent statement that the configurations themselves possess a universal measurable difference.
content.definition_indistinguishability: Two configurations are observer-relative indistinguishable when their effective distinction falls below the observer's resolution threshold:
content.definition_distinguishability: They are observer-relative distinguishable when the effective distinction reaches or exceeds that threshold:
content.threshold_boundary: The threshold is inclusive on the distinguishable side. A distinction equal to \(I_N(O)\) is therefore resolvable by \(O\). No universal numerical value for \(I_N\) is assumed at this foundational stage.
content.relational_interpretation: The relation is explicitly indexed by \(O\) because resolution is observer-relative rather than universal. In general, it is permitted that \(I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2)\), and consequently that the same pair \((x,y)\) is distinguishable to \(O_1\) while being indistinguishable to \(O_2\). This does not imply that the pair has changed. Only the observer-relative resolution relation has changed.
content.non_erasure: Observer-relative indistinguishability must not be confused with ontological identity, nonexistence, deletion, or removal from the Library. From \(x \approx_O y\) it does not follow that \(x=y\). Nor does it follow that either configuration is absent from \(\mathcal{M}\). Formally:
content.static_totality_preservation: Because \(\mathcal{M}\) is treated as a static totality, observer-relative resolution cannot modify Library membership. For any observer \(O\), changing \(I_N(O)\), changing the observer's history, or changing the observer's current relational reference may alter which distinctions are operationally available, but none of these operations constitutes a change to \(\mathcal{M}\) itself.
content.operational_vs_ontological: Two distinct relations must therefore be kept separate. Library membership is ontological within the formal model: \(x \in \mathcal{M}\). Observer-relative distinguishability is operational and relational: whether \(O\) can maintain the distinction between \(x\) and \(y\) above \(I_N(O)\). Observer-relative accessibility is consequently a relation over the Library, not a criterion that determines which configurations belong to it.
content.example: Suppose \(x,y \in \mathcal{M}\) and \(x \neq y\). If \(\delta_O(x,y) < I_N(O)\), then \(O\) cannot maintain their difference as a resolved distinction. For \(O\), the two configurations therefore occupy the same effective resolution class. Nevertheless, the Library has not identified \(x\) and \(y\) as equal, and neither configuration has been removed from \(\mathcal{M}\). A different observer \(O'\), with a different resolution threshold or relational structure, may resolve the distinction.
content.resolution_classes: Observer-relative distinguishability can be represented as a family of resolution classes induced by the threshold \(I_N(O)\). Configurations whose effective distinctions fall below that threshold may be grouped together operationally for \(O\), even when they remain distinct members of \(\mathcal{M}\). These resolution classes therefore belong to the observer-relative description of the Library and must not be reified as partitions that alter the underlying totality.
content.reference_independence: The existence of an observer-relative resolution relation does not privilege the observer's current configuration as a universal origin of the Library. The observer may evaluate distinctions from a particular relational reference, but that reference does not establish a boundary around \(\mathcal{M}\) and does not determine which configurations exist. The whole Library remains the unchanged domain over which observer-relative distinctions are evaluated.
content.handoff: A distinction becomes structurally important when it remains resolvable across successive transitions. The next step is therefore persistence: rather than asking only whether \(O\) can distinguish \(x\) from \(y\), we ask whether \(O\) can maintain a chain of resolvable distinctions without treating sub-threshold distinctions as ontological disappearance.

mathematics.membership_invariance: x \in \mathcal{M} \text{ is independent of whether } x \text{ is distinguishable to } O
mathematics.resolution_relation: \approx_O \text{ is an observer-relative operational relation over } \mathcal{M}

formal_consequences: Distinguishability is a relation involving configurations and an observer.
The threshold \(I_N(O)\) is observer-relative rather than a universal constant.
Sub-threshold distinction does not imply equality.
Sub-threshold distinction does not imply destruction, deletion, or removal from the Library.
Observer-relative resolution does not alter the static membership of \(\mathcal{M}\).
Ontological membership \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) and observer-relative distinguishability are distinct concepts.
Observer-relative accessibility is induced over \(\mathcal{M}\) rather than constituting \(\mathcal{M}\).
A configuration can remain in \(\mathcal{M}\) while failing to be operationally distinguishable by \(O\).
Different observers may induce different resolution classes over the same unchanged Library.
Changing observer resolution changes the relational description available to the observer, not the underlying totality.
prohibited_inferences: Do not interpret \(x \approx_O y\) as \(x=y\).
Do not interpret observer-relative indistinguishability as destruction, deletion, or ontological disappearance.
Do not interpret observer-relative resolution as a mechanism that generates or modifies Library membership.
Do not claim that the observer creates or determines the underlying configuration.
Do not treat the observer's current reference configuration as a privileged universal origin of \(\mathcal{M}\).
Do not introduce consciousness as a condition for distinguishability.
Do not assign a universal numerical value to \(I_N\).
Do not identify \(I_N(O)\) with the ordinary Planck scale at this stage.
Do not interpret the abstract distinction relation as physical measurement before a physical interpretation is separately introduced.
Do not convert observer-relative resolution classes into ontological partitions of the Library.
Do not infer that inaccessible configurations cease to belong to the static totality.

subsections.title: Persistence Across Successive Distinctions and Observer-Relative Coherence
subsections.purpose: Extend single-transition distinguishability into a persistent sequence, establish observerhood as a structural capacity rather than a primitive, and prepare the formal transition from persistence to coherence as an observer-, history-, and reference-relative relation over the unchanged Library.
subsections.poetic_cypher: One distinction may appear; a chain of distinctions can remain. The whole is the field; the point is the question.
subsections.cypher_explanation: Persistence identifies the structural capacity to maintain resolvable distinctions across an abstractly ordered sequence. Once such a structure is available, coherence is not assigned intrinsically to a path. It is evaluated relationally with respect to an observer, its relevant history, and its current relational reference within the whole Library.

content.sequence: Let \\gamma=(x_0,x_1,\\ldots,x_n) be a finite sequence of configurations in \\mathcal{M}. The index i is an abstract ordering index and is not identified with physical time.
content.static_domain: Every x_i belongs to the same unchanged Library \\mathcal{M}. The sequence does not represent the progressive creation of Library states. It represents an ordered relational traversal through configurations that are already members of the static totality.
content.step_condition: A transition from x_i to x_{i+1} is resolvable by O when \\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) \\geq I_N(O).
content.interpretation: A sequence is persistent for O when every successive distinction in the sequence remains above O's observer-relative resolution floor. Persistence does not require physical motion, temporal evolution, causality, or an ontological transition between successive Library states. It is a structural property of an ordered sequence of resolvable distinctions.
content.observerhood: Observerhood is derived structurally from the capacity to maintain persistent distinguishability. An observer is not introduced as a primitive subject imposed from outside the Library. Rather, an observer-capable structure is identified wherever a configuration or relational structure can maintain a persistent chain of distinctions relative to its observer-specific resolution condition.
content.observer_definition: O\\in\\mathrm{Obs}\\subseteq\\mathcal{M} \\iff O\\text{ is capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions satisfying }\\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})\\geq I_N(O).
content.no_consciousness_requirement: Nothing in this definition requires consciousness, perception, intention, agency, or a human subject. Observerhood names a structural capacity to preserve distinguishability across an abstractly ordered sequence.
content.no_birth_event: The identification of an observer does not represent a physical birth event or a temporal transition in the Library. It is a structural designation made within the static totality. The observer-capable relation is present wherever the relevant persistent distinguishability structure exists.
content.whole_library_relation: The observer established by persistent distinguishability is not thereby confined to a locally generated region of \\mathcal{M}. Its subsequent coherence relation is evaluated over paths in the whole Library. The Library remains unchanged while the observer-relative relation over it varies.
content.reference_dependence: Where coherence depends on a current relational reference, write the coherence relation as \\mathcal{C}(\\gamma\\mid O,h,x), where O denotes the observer structure, h denotes the relevant observer history, and x denotes the current observer-relative reference configuration. These parameters modify the relational evaluation; they do not modify Library membership.
content.coherence_transition: Persistence establishes that successive distinctions can remain resolvable. Coherence extends this relation from individual transitions to paths evaluated relative to O, h, and x. Thus coherence is not an intrinsic property of \\gamma independent of reference.
content.whole_library_path_domain: Candidate paths are drawn from \\mathrm{Path}(\\mathcal{M}), the path structure of the unchanged totality. Observer-relative coherence selects a subset of these paths; it does not construct, delete, or redefine the Library.
content.nonempty_continuation_requirement: Under the combined NSFG structural assumptions, every admissible observer-relative reference configuration x\\in\\mathcal{M}_{\\mathrm{admissible}} is required to admit at least one coherent continuation above the relevant observer-dependent coherence floor. This requirement is a derived structural condition and is not claimed to follow from maximality alone.
content.handoff: Persistence supplies the bridge from isolated distinguishability to observerhood. The next construction therefore treats coherence as a relational evaluation over the unchanged whole Library, with observer, history, and current reference determining which paths remain coherent for traversal.

mathematics.structural_observer_condition: O\\in\\mathrm{Obs} \\iff O\\text{ can maintain a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions}
mathematics.reference_invariance: x\\mapsto x'\\text{ changes the observer-relative relational evaluation but does not change }\\mathcal{M}

formal_consequences: Persistence is defined over an abstract sequence, not physical time.
The sequence index does not describe the creation or evolution of successive Library states.
Every configuration in the sequence remains a member of the same static totality \\mathcal{M}.
Persistence requires repeated resolvability rather than a single distinguishable transition.
Observerhood is derived from persistent distinguishability rather than introduced as an additional primitive axiom.
Observerhood does not imply consciousness, perception, agency, or intentionality.
The observer-relative threshold remains specific to the observer through I_N(O).
Coherence is not intrinsic to a path independently of observer and relational reference.
Coherence is evaluated over Path(\\mathcal{M}), not over a locally generated neighborhood.
Changing observer history or reference changes the relational coherence structure without changing Library membership.
The existence of a coherent continuation from every admissible reference configuration is a derived structural requirement of the combined model assumptions, not a theorem of maximality alone.
prohibited_inferences: Do not identify the sequence index i with physical time.
Do not interpret persistence as physical motion or causal evolution.
Do not interpret successive configurations as successive versions of the Library.
Do not describe observerhood as the physical birth of a subject.
Do not equate observerhood with consciousness.
Do not introduce agency, intention, or privileged selection.
Do not treat observerhood as an additional primitive axiom.
Do not treat coherence as an intrinsic property of an isolated path.
Do not treat the observer as confined to a locally generated neighborhood of the Library.
Do not allow observer resolution or coherence to determine Library membership.
Do not claim that maximality alone proves the existence of a coherent continuation from every admissible reference configuration.

semantic_separation.library: \\mathcal{M} is the static, maximally complete total configuration domain.
semantic_separation.observer: O is an observer-capable relational structure identified by persistent distinguishability.
semantic_separation.history: h is the observer-relative ordered history relevant to the current relational evaluation.
semantic_separation.reference: x is the current observer-relative reference configuration and may be any admissible configuration in \\mathcal{M}.
semantic_separation.coherence: \\mathcal{C}(\\gamma\\mid O,h,x) is an observer-relative relation over paths in \\mathcal{M}.
