sections.title: Coherence Is Relational
sections.purpose: Establish observer-relative coherence as a derived relation rather than a universal scalar.
sections.poetic_cipher: Coherence is not inside the path. It is between the path and the survivor.
sections.cipher_explanation: Coherence does not belong intrinsically to a path considered in isolation. It is a relation between a path's transitions and an observer O whose resolution threshold determines whether those transitions remain distinguishable. The word 'survivor' refers here to an observer-like configuration already defined structurally by persistent distinguishability; it does not imply consciousness, intention, or agency.
sections.content: Coherence is introduced only after distinguishability, persistence, observerhood, and observer-relative resolution have been established. The axiomatic floor therefore does not begin by assigning a universal coherence value to configurations or paths. Instead, coherence is derived from a prior question: does a given transition remain distinguishable to a particular observer O at that observer's available resolution? This distinction is essential. A path is not coherent or incoherent in itself. The same transition may be resolvable by one observer and unresolved by another if their resolution thresholds differ. Coherence is consequently written as a relation between a path and an observer, \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\), rather than as an observer-independent property \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma)\). At this stage, coherence is deliberately defined as a threshold relation rather than as a physical field, probability, force, or dynamical quantity. No physical law is required to establish the relation. The only ingredients are an observer-relative distinguishability function \(\delta_O\), the observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\), and an elementary threshold function. The result is a binary criterion: a transition either remains resolvable at the observer's threshold or it does not. This construction also preserves the distinction between ontological membership and observer accessibility. A transition that fails the coherence criterion for O is not thereby removed from the Library. It simply fails to remain accessible to that observer under the defined resolution condition. Coherence therefore acts as a relational filter on traversal, not as an erasure rule for configurations.

subsections.title: Coherence of a Transition
subsections.purpose: Define coherence for an individual transition using only the observer-relative distinguishability function and the observer-relative resolution threshold.
subsections.content:
Let \(O\) be an observer-like configuration and let \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) be two successive configurations in an abstractly ordered sequence. By the preceding construction, the effective distinction between these configurations as resolved by O is represented by \(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})\), while the minimum effective distinction that O can maintain as a stable distinction is represented by \(I_N(O)\). A transition is coherent for O precisely when its effective distinction meets or exceeds the observer's resolution threshold. The coherence relation is therefore defined by \[
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = \Theta\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) - I_N(O)\right).
\] Here, \(\Theta\) is the elementary threshold function defined by \[
\Theta(z) =
\begin{cases}
1, & z \geq 0,\\
0, & z < 0.
\end{cases}
\] It follows directly that \[
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) = 1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}) \geq I_N(O).
\] The threshold is therefore not an additional universal property of the transition. It enters through the observer. If two observers \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) possess different resolution thresholds, then the same transition may satisfy \[
\delta_{O_1}(x_i,x_{i+1}) \geq I_N(O_1)
\] while simultaneously failing \[
\delta_{O_2}(x_i,x_{i+1}) < I_N(O_2).
\] In that case, the transition is coherent relative to \(O_1\) but not coherent relative to \(O_2\). Nothing contradictory has occurred: coherence was never defined as an absolute property of the transition. This observer dependence does not mean that the observer creates the underlying configurations or determines whether they belong to the Library. Membership in the Library remains an ontological statement about the formal closure. Coherence instead determines whether a distinction between configurations survives at the resolution available to a particular observer. The role of \(I_N(O)\) is therefore that of a resolution floor. It determines the boundary between distinctions that O can maintain and distinctions that fall below O's effective resolution. No universal numerical value is assigned to \(I_N(O)\), and no identification with the ordinary Planck scale is made at this foundational stage. The distinction between transition coherence and path coherence must also be preserved. A single coherent transition does not establish that an entire path is coherent. A path contains a sequence of transitions, and each transition must independently satisfy the observer-relative coherence condition. The next construction therefore extends \(\mathcal{C}_O\) from individual transitions to the coherence of an entire path.

mathematics.observer_dependence: \(\mathcal{C}_{O_1}(x_i,x_{i+1})\) and \(\mathcal{C}_{O_2}(x_i,x_{i+1})\) may differ when \(I_N(O_1) \neq I_N(O_2)\) or when their distinguishability functions differ.

interpretive_boundary: Coherence is a relation, not an intrinsic scalar attached to an isolated path.
The observer-relative threshold \(I_N(O)\) determines whether a transition remains resolvable for O.
Failure of coherence for O does not remove the transition or its configurations from the Library.
Observer-relative coherence does not imply that an observer creates or alters the underlying configuration.
No consciousness, agency, intention, physical time, causality, matter, energy, or physical law is required by this definition.
subsections.poetic_cipher: Coherence is not inside the path. It is between the path and the survivor.
subsections.cipher_explanation: The 'path' denotes an ordered sequence of configurations, while the 'survivor' denotes the observer-like configuration whose persistent distinguishability has already been established. A transition is coherent only when its distinction remains above that observer's resolution threshold. The cipher therefore compresses the relational structure \(\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1})\) without introducing a new primitive.
subsections.handoff: A coherent transition is insufficient to establish coherent traversal. A path contains multiple transitions, so path coherence requires the observer-relative coherence condition to hold across the entire sequence.

content.text: Coherence is defined here as a property of the relation between a path and an observer, not as an intrinsic property of the path alone. Let a path be an abstract finite sequence of configurations \(\gamma=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), where each \(x_i\in\mathcal{M}\). The sequence index \(i\) denotes abstract ordering only; it is not yet physical time.
content.definition: For an observer \(O\), let the coherence of each transition be defined by \(\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1})=\Theta\!\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1})-I_N(O)\right)\). Path coherence is then the product of the coherence of every transition along the path:
content.interpretation: Because each factor is either 0 or 1, the product is 1 exactly when every transition in the path remains resolvable by observer \(O\). If even one transition falls below the observer's resolution threshold \(I_N(O)\), the corresponding factor is 0 and the path is incoherent for that observer.
content.observer_dependence: This definition makes observer dependence explicit. Two observers may assign different coherence values to the same path because their resolution thresholds and effective distinguishability functions may differ. Thus, for observers \(O_1\) and \(O_2\), it is permitted that \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O_1)\neq\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O_2)\). A path can therefore be coherent for one observer while being incoherent for another without any contradiction.
content.no_universal_coherence: There is consequently no universal coherence constant supplied by the axiomatic floor. Coherence is not a fixed scalar belonging to \(\gamma\) independently of its observer. The meaningful foundational object is the relation \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\): the coherence of path \(\gamma\) relative to observer \(O\). Any later theory that assigns a universal numerical coherence parameter would require additional axioms and cannot be inferred from the present construction alone.
content.formal_consequence: The distinction is important because the Library itself remains unfiltered. A path for which \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=0\) has not been removed from \(\mathcal{M}\). It has merely failed the coherence condition relative to that observer. Coherence therefore determines accessibility rather than ontological membership.
content.boundary: At this stage, coherence does not describe physical stability, causal consistency, energetic feasibility, or any other physical law. It describes only whether the successive distinctions along a path remain resolvable relative to a specified observer.
content.poetic_cipher: The same road may be solid beneath one traveler and vanish beneath another.
content.cipher_explanation: The road represents the path \(\gamma\). Its being solid represents \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=1\), meaning that every transition remains resolvable for the observer. Its vanishing represents \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)=0\), meaning that at least one transition falls below the observer's resolution threshold. Different travelers represent different observers with potentially different resolution capacities. The metaphor therefore expresses observer-relative coherence without introducing an additional primitive.
content.handoff: If coherence is relational, then each observer traverses only a subset of the Library through paths that remain coherent relative to that observer. This motivates the next construction: the observer-accessible subset \(A_O\subseteq\mathcal{M}\), which provides the formal basis for observer-accessible reality.

interpretive_claims: The same path may be coherent for one observer and incoherent for another.
Coherence should be represented relationally as \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O)\).

sections.title: Accessible Reality
sections.purpose: Define observer-relative experienced reality without making observers creators of the Library.
sections.poetic_cipher: The world does not shrink. The window does.
sections.cipher_explanation: The Library remains the full XOR closure 𝓜. Observer-relative reality is not a reduction of that closure, but the subset of configurations through which a given observer can maintain coherent traversal. Accessibility therefore describes a relation between an observer and the Library rather than a change to the Library itself.
sections.introduction: The Library, 𝓜, is defined at the axiomatic floor as the closure of the formal domain under the primitive operation XOR. Its membership is therefore ontological within the formal system: a configuration either belongs to 𝓜 or it does not. Observer-relative accessibility introduces a different question. Rather than asking whether a configuration exists within the Library, we ask whether that configuration can occur within a path whose distinctions remain resolvable by a particular observer O. This distinction is essential. Accessibility is a property of an observer-Library relation; it is not a criterion for membership in the Library itself.

subsections.title: Accessibility Is Not Existence
subsections.purpose: Define observer-relative accessibility over the unchanged Library while formally establishing arbitrary observer-relative reference. This section separates ontological membership in the static totality from observer-relative traversal, and introduces the Reference-Point Coherence Proposition as a derived structural requirement rather than a theorem of maximality alone.
subsections.poetic_cipher: The world does not shrink. The window does. Any point may become the center, and the whole must still resolve into a path.
subsections.cipher_explanation: The 'world' refers to the full Library \(\mathcal{M}\), which remains a single static, eternally maximally complete totality. The 'window' refers to the observer-relative accessibility relation, which changes with observer, history, resolution, and current relational reference without changing Library membership. The second clause expresses reference-point neutrality: no configuration is privileged as the universal origin of traversal. An admissible configuration may serve as the observer-relative reference, and the model requires that coherent continuation remain available from that reference without altering the underlying totality.

content.definition: Let \(O\) be an observer, meaning a configuration capable of maintaining a persistent chain of distinctions above its observer-relative resolution threshold \(I_N(O)\). Let \(h\) denote the observer history relevant to the current relational evaluation, and let \(x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}}\) be an admissible reference configuration. The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library \(\mathcal{M}\), rather than ontologically confined to a local region of it. Accessibility is therefore defined by the existence of observer-relative coherent traversal from the reference \(x\), given \(O\) and \(h\).

mathematics.admissible_reference_configuration: \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}} := \{x \in \mathcal{M} \mid x\text{ can instantiate an observer-relative reference state under the model's admissibility conditions}\}\)
mathematics.noise_threshold: \(\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\) denotes the minimum coherence distinguishable or sustainable by observer \(O\) under the relevant resolution condition.
mathematics.accessible_states: \(A_O(h,x) = \{y \in \mathcal{M} \mid \exists\gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\text{ beginning at }(h,x)\text{ and containing }y\text{ such that }\mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x) > \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\}\)
mathematics.reference_point_coherence_proposition: \(\forall x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\ \forall(O,h)\text{ compatible with }x,\ \exists\gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M}): \gamma\text{ begins at }(h,x) \land \mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x) > \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\)

content.interpretation: The condition \(y \in \mathcal{M}\) concerns ontological membership in the static Library. The condition \(y \in A_O(h,x)\) concerns accessibility through an observer-relative coherent traversal relation. These conditions are therefore not equivalent. A configuration may belong to \(\mathcal{M}\) while remaining inaccessible to a particular observer from a particular reference and history. Conversely, every configuration in \(A_O(h,x)\) is already a member of \(\mathcal{M}\).
content.ontological_membership: Membership in \(\mathcal{M}\) is determined by the formal characterization of the Library through XOR closure. The closure relation establishes the mathematical structure of the totality; it is not a temporal generation process. Traversal does not generate new Library configurations, and observer resolution does not determine Library membership.
content.static_totality: The Library is a single static, eternally maximally complete totality. It is not progressively generated, expanded, depleted, or modified as an observer traverses it. The notation \(\mathcal{M}_i = \mathcal{M}\) is therefore an invariance statement and does not represent successive physical copies of the Library.
content.observer_relative_traversal: Accessibility is observer-relative because coherence is evaluated as \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x)\). Changing the observer, its relevant history, its resolution, or its current relational reference may change the accessible subset without changing \(\mathcal{M}\). The observer's current reference determines the experienced traversal relation, not the existence or membership of configurations.
content.whole_library_relation: The observer is not defined as occupying a local ontological region of \(\mathcal{M}\). Rather, the observer is a configuration relationally situated with respect to the whole totality while maintaining a restricted coherent continuation relation. Thus, observer-relative locality belongs to the traversal structure, not to a partition of the Library into intrinsically local regions.
content.non_erasure_principle: If \(y \notin A_O(h,x)\), this establishes only that \(y\) is not contained in the observer-accessible subset under the stated accessibility criterion. It does not establish \(y \notin \mathcal{M}\). Inaccessibility is therefore not erasure.
content.anti_idealism_constraint: This construction does not assert that observers create, determine, or constitute the Library. The observer does not bring inaccessible configurations into existence by resolving them, nor does failure to resolve a configuration remove it from \(\mathcal{M}\). Observer-relative accessibility concerns traversal, distinguishability, and coherence over an unchanged totality, not ontological creation.
content.reference_point_neutrality: No configuration is privileged as the universal starting point of coherent traversal. If \(x\) and \(x'\) are both admissible observer-relative reference configurations, changing the reference changes the relational evaluation but does not alter the Library. A privileged construction origin would introduce an asymmetry into traversal that is not present in the foundational ontology.
content.reference_point_coherence: The Reference-Point Coherence Proposition states the required structural condition that every admissible observer-relative reference configuration must admit at least one coherent continuation. This proposition is not claimed to follow from maximality alone. It follows from the combined NSFG assumptions of maximal static totality, reference-point neutrality, whole-Library relationality, and the requirement that coherent traversal remain possible from an arbitrary admissible reference.
content.proof_status: The Reference-Point Coherence Proposition is a derived model requirement. Maximality establishes that no admissible configuration is excluded merely because it is not part of a privileged construction history; it does not by itself prove that a coherent continuation exists from every reference. Nonempty continuation is imposed by the combined structural requirement that arbitrary admissible observer-relative reference remain capable of coherent traversal.
content.experienced_reality: For the purposes of the primer, the observer-relative experienced reality may therefore be named \(R_O(h,x) := A_O(h,x)\). This notation does not imply that \(A_O(h,x)\) is the whole of \(\mathcal{M}\). It identifies the portion of the unchanged Library that is accessible through coherent traversal relative to observer \(O\), relevant history \(h\), and reference \(x\).
content.temporal_boundary: No intrinsic past/future partition is introduced into \(\mathcal{M}\). The sequence of configurations encountered by an observer constitutes an ordering of traversal relative to its history and reference. Apparent temporal sequence therefore belongs to the observer-relative relation over the Library rather than to an ontological evolution of the Library itself.
content.complexity_boundary: Likewise, an observer may experience increasing complexity, locality, or differentiation as its relational history changes, but this does not imply that \(\mathcal{M}\) itself evolves from simpler to more complex states. The totality remains unchanged while the observer's relation to it changes.
content.formal_boundary: At this stage, no claim is made that \(A_O(h,x)\) corresponds directly to human sensory experience, phenomenal consciousness, or a complete physical universe. It is a formal construction describing observer-relative accessibility within the Library. Likewise, no physical temporal direction is assumed by the ordering of a path.

derivation.statement: The Library is characterized mathematically by \(\mathcal{M} := \operatorname{Closure}_D(\oplus)\), while the closure relation is explicitly not interpreted as temporal generation.
The Library is treated as a single static totality satisfying \(\forall i,\ \mathcal{M}_i = \mathcal{M}\).
An admissible reference configuration is defined as an \(x \in \mathcal{M}\) capable of instantiating an observer-relative reference state under the model's admissibility conditions.
For observer \(O\), history \(h\), and reference \(x\), coherence is evaluated relationally as \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x)\).
derivation.status: previously established construction, extended by explicit reference dependence

derivation.statement: A configuration \(y\) is accessible when it occurs on at least one path through \(\mathcal{M}\) beginning from \((h,x)\) whose coherence exceeds the observer's relevant noise threshold \(\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\).
Therefore \(A_O(h,x)\subseteq\mathcal{M}\), and defining the accessible subset does not modify the Library.
Changing the observer-relative reference from \(x\) to another admissible reference \(x'\) changes the relational accessibility structure but leaves \(\mathcal{M}\) invariant.
Because no admissible reference is privileged as the universal origin of traversal, the model requires that every admissible reference configuration admit at least one coherent continuation.

The resulting Reference-Point Coherence Proposition is therefore \(\forall x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\ \forall(O,h)\text{ compatible with }x,\ \exists\gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M}): \gamma\text{ begins at }(h,x) \land \mathcal{C}(\gamma \mid O,h,x) > \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\).
derivation.status: derived requirement, not theorem from maximality alone

derivation.statement: The observer-relative accessible subset can be identified with experienced reality as \(R_O(h,x):=A_O(h,x)\), without identifying that subset with the total Library.

example.setup: Suppose \(x\) and \(y\) are both configurations in the unchanged Library \(\mathcal{M}\), and suppose \(x\) is an admissible observer-relative reference configuration. Assume there exists a path \(\gamma_x\) beginning from \((h,x)\) whose coherence satisfies \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma_x \mid O,h,x)>\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\), while no currently accessible O-coherent path from \((h,x)\) contains \(y\).
example.result: Then \(x \in \mathcal{M}\), \(y \in \mathcal{M}\), and \(y \notin A_O(h,x)\), while the coherent continuation from \(x\) remains available.
example.interpretation: The distinction demonstrates that accessibility is not existence. The observer's traversal from \(x\) selects a restricted relational subset of the unchanged totality; it does not generate that subset as new ontology. Likewise, the observer's inability to access \(y\) does not remove \(y\) from \(\mathcal{M}\). If another admissible reference \(x'\) is selected, the accessible relation may differ while the Library remains exactly the same.
example.reference_point_variant: Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) be two admissible reference configurations. The model does not permit either one to function as a privileged universal origin. The observer-relative continuation relation may differ between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), but both are evaluated over the same \(\mathcal{M}\), and the structural requirement is that each admit at least one coherent continuation.

invariants: \(\mathcal{M}\) is a single static, eternally maximally complete totality.
\(\forall i,\ \mathcal{M}_i = \mathcal{M}\).
Mathematical closure does not represent temporal generation.
Observer traversal does not add to or remove from Library membership.
The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole Library.
The observer-relative reference configuration does not define an ontological locality of the Library.
Changing the admissible reference changes the observer-relative relation but does not alter \(\mathcal{M}\).
No privileged worldline or universal construction origin is assumed.
\(A_O(h,x)\) is observer-, history-, and reference-relative.
\(A_O(h,x) \subseteq \mathcal{M}\).
\(y \notin A_O(h,x)\) does not imply \(y \notin \mathcal{M}\).
Accessibility does not create ontological membership.
Inaccessibility does not erase ontological membership.
The Reference-Point Coherence Proposition is a derived model requirement, not a theorem of maximality alone.
Every admissible reference configuration is required to admit at least one coherent continuation.
No intrinsic past/future partition is introduced into \(\mathcal{M}\).
Apparent temporal and complexity ordering belongs to observer-relative traversal rather than Library evolution.
Experienced reality \(R_O(h,x):=A_O(h,x)\) is a relational construction.
No privileged observer is required.
No consciousness requirement is introduced.
subsections.handoff: The distinction is now explicit: \(\mathcal{M}\) is the unchanged totality, \(O(h)\) is the observer's current configuration and relevant history, and \(A_O(h,x)\) is the observer-relative accessible relation over that totality. Because arbitrary admissible reference configurations are required to admit coherent continuation without generating new Library content, the next section can instantiate the continuation space directly over the unchanged \(\mathcal{M}\).

subsections.title: Observer-Relative Reality
subsections.content:
Experienced reality is defined here as the subset of the Library that is accessible to a particular observer through a coherent path. For observer O, we therefore define experienced reality as R_O := A_O, where A_O is the observer-accessible subset established in the preceding section. This definition does not assert that the observer creates the accessible configurations. It states only that the configurations available through observer-relative coherent traversal constitute that observer's experienced reality. The ontological domain remains the Library 𝓜, while experienced reality is a subset of that domain. Because the resolution threshold I_N(O) is observer-relative, there is no requirement that all observers have identical accessible subsets. Let the collection of observers be Obs = {O_1,O_2,...}. For each observer O_i, the corresponding experienced reality is R_i = A_{O_i}. Two observers may therefore traverse overlapping but non-identical regions of the Library. This difference follows from the relational construction of distinguishability and coherence: what remains resolvable and coherently traversable for one observer need not be identical to what remains resolvable and coherently traversable for another. The common portion of two observer-relative realities is represented by their intersection: \[
R_{ij} = R_i \cap R_j.
\] The set R_{ij} contains configurations accessible to both observers. A non-empty intersection therefore provides a formal basis for shared reality without requiring the two observers to possess identical accessible domains. Conversely, the observer-relative difference between their accessible realities can be represented by the symmetric difference: \[
D_{ij} = R_i \triangle R_j.
\] The set D_{ij} contains configurations accessible to one observer but not the other. Such a difference should not be interpreted as evidence that the observers inhabit mutually incompatible ontological universes. Both R_i and R_j remain subsets of the same Library 𝓜: \[
R_i \subseteq \mathcal{M}, \qquad R_j \subseteq \mathcal{M}.
\] Thus, observer-relative reality describes a difference in access, resolution, and coherent survivability rather than a difference in fundamental existence. A configuration may belong to 𝓜 while being inaccessible to one observer, accessible to another, or accessible to both. Inaccessibility therefore remains a relational property and does not constitute ontological erasure. This distinction also prevents observer-relative reality from collapsing into a claim of arbitrary subjectivity. The observer does not freely select an arbitrary reality. Accessibility is constrained by the formal structure of 𝓜, the observer's distinguishability relation δ_O, the observer-relative threshold I_N(O), and the requirement that coherent paths remain resolvable. Different observers may consequently obtain different accessible subsets while still sharing substantial structure because their coherent path spaces overlap within the same underlying Library. The construction can therefore be summarized as follows: the Library specifies the total formal configuration domain; each observer induces an observer-relative accessibility relation over that domain; and experienced reality is the resulting accessible subset. Reality is observer-relative at the level of access, but not thereby observer-created at the level of ontology.

mathematics.interpretation: R_{ij} represents shared accessible structure, while D_{ij} represents observer-relative difference in accessibility.

subsections.poetic_cypher: Many windows can face one Library without making one window the sky.
subsections.cypher_explanation: The windows represent observers and their observer-relative accessible realities R_i. The Library represents the common ontological domain 𝓜. Different windows may reveal different portions of that domain, and their views may overlap, but no individual window becomes the Library itself. The metaphor therefore compresses the distinction between observer-relative access and underlying ontological membership without introducing a competing ontology.
subsections.formal_status: The definition R_O := A_O and the set-theoretic relations among R_i, R_{ij}, D_{ij}, and 𝓜 are formal constructions. The interpretation of these constructions as experienced reality is an observer-relative interpretation of the accessibility framework, not an additional axiom.
subsections.handoff: Once accessible reality is defined, we can examine why stable patterns within it can appear as physical laws.

sections.section_summary: Accessible reality is the observer-relative subset A_O of the Library through which coherent traversal can be maintained. The definition changes neither the Library nor its membership. It establishes a formal distinction between existence within 𝓜 and accessibility relative to O, allowing experienced reality to be represented as R_O := A_O without adopting subjective idealism or making the observer a creator of reality.
sections.section_boundary: This section establishes accessibility only. It does not yet introduce emergent physical law, probabilistic dynamics, consciousness, physical time, or cosmological interpretation.

sections.title: Survivorship and Emergent Lawfulness
sections.purpose: Explain how law-like regularity can arise without being imposed as an axiom.
sections.poetic_cypher: What survives need not be commanded; what survives repeatedly becomes a pattern.
sections.cypher_explanation: The poetic statement compresses the distinction between axiomatic law and observed regularity. No law governing traversal is introduced into the axiomatic floor. Instead, the Library contains an unfiltered configuration domain, while observer-relative coherence restricts which continuations can remain accessible to a particular observer O. When the same accessible transitions recur across an appropriate family of observer-accessible paths, the recurrence can be described as a regularity. Such regularity is derived from survivorship and is therefore descriptive rather than axiomatic.
formal_dependency: The Library is defined independently of survivorship as the XOR closure 𝓜 := Closure_D(⊕).
For a configuration x ∈ 𝓜, the continuation space Ω(x) represents available configuration continuations contained in 𝓜.
For an observer O, the coherent subset Ω_O^survive(x) selects those continuations whose paths remain resolvable by O.
Repeatedly surviving transitions can therefore form stable observable patterns without requiring a law to be inserted into the axiomatic floor.

subsections.title: The Unfiltered Continuation Space
subsections.purpose: Define continuation as an observer-relative ordering over the already-complete Library rather than as a locally generated future neighborhood. The total candidate path space is defined over Path(𝓜), with the current configuration x serving as the observer's relational reference. Observer-relative coherence then selects a nonempty surviving continuation subset without altering Library membership.
content: Let x ∈ 𝓜 be an admissible observer-relative reference configuration. Because 𝓜 is a static, eternally maximally complete totality, x does not mark the beginning of a newly generated region of the Library, nor does it define an ontological boundary between a present and a future.
The candidate continuation space is therefore defined over the whole path space of the unchanged Library. Let Path(𝓜) denote the set of configuration paths represented within 𝓜.
Define the unfiltered continuation space from reference configuration x by:
Ω(x) = {γ ∈ Path(𝓜) | γ begins at x}.

Ω(x) is unfiltered with respect to observer-relative coherence. It is not a locally generated neighborhood and does not represent a collection of future events waiting to be created. It is the subset of the already-complete relational path structure whose paths have x as their current reference.
More generally, when an observer has an accumulated history h ending at x, continuation must be evaluated relative to both that history and the current reference:
Γ_O(h,x) = {γ ∈ Path(𝓜) | γ extends h from x and 𝓒(γ | O,h,x) > γ_noise}.
Here Γ_O(h,x) is not a second ontology and does not replace Ω(x). It is the observer-relative coherent continuation relation induced over the unchanged totality 𝓜.

The distinction is therefore between the existence of candidate paths in the totality and their maintainability as coherent traversal for a particular observer. A path may belong to Path(𝓜), and therefore to Ω(x) when it begins at x, while failing to belong to Γ_O(h,x) because its continuation cannot be maintained above the observer's relevant coherence threshold.

The observer's reference point does not alter 𝓜. Changing x changes which paths are considered as continuations from that relational reference and may change the observer-relative coherence relation, but it does not add configurations to the Library or remove configurations from it.

This permits an arbitrary admissible configuration to function as the current relational reference without introducing a privileged starting configuration. A construction in which coherent continuation existed only from a distinguished origin would implicitly privilege that origin as a universal worldline.

The NSFG requirement is therefore not that every candidate continuation be coherent. Rather, under the model's assumptions, every admissible observer-relative reference must admit at least one coherent continuation:
∀x ∈ 𝓜_admissible, Γ_O(h,x) ≠ ∅.
This nonempty-continuation condition is a derived structural requirement of the combined NSFG assumptions. It is not asserted to follow from maximality alone.

Accordingly, observer traversal is a restricted relational ordering over the whole Library. The observer experiences a continuation from x because some paths through the totality remain coherent relative to O, h, and x; the Library itself does not generate those paths at the moment of traversal.

The apparent distinction between a current position and its continuation is therefore observer-relative rather than an ontological partition of 𝓜 into present and future regions. Past and future are ordering relations induced by traversal, while the total configuration domain remains unchanged.

Inaccessibility or incoherence under O does not imply non-existence in 𝓜. The complement of the observer-maintained coherent continuation set remains part of the total configuration and path structure.

subsections.title: Repeated Survivorship
subsections.purpose: Explain how recurrence among observer-accessible transitions can be identified without treating recurrence itself as an axiom, while preserving the distinction between observer-relative survivorship and Library membership.
content: Consider a family of paths evaluated relative to an observer O, its relevant history h, and current reference configuration x. These paths are drawn from the unchanged total path domain Path(𝓜). A transition that repeatedly survives observer-relative coherence across an appropriate family of such paths can exhibit stable recurrence relative to O.

Survivorship therefore operates on traversal relations, not on the ontology of the Library. A transition may fail to remain coherent for observer O without the configurations or candidate paths involved thereby being removed from 𝓜 or from the total path domain. The incoherent complement remains represented in the Library; only its continuation through the observer-maintained coherent relation is not retained as part of that traversal.

The important distinction is between requiring a transition and observing that a transition repeatedly survives. The former would introduce a governing rule into the axiomatic floor; the latter is a descriptive identification of a stable pattern within the relational structure produced by observer-relative coherence.

Thus, a transition does not become regular because an external law commands it to occur. It becomes law-like when its recurrence is stable across an appropriate observer-accessible ensemble. Such regularity is therefore derived from repeated survivorship rather than imposed upon the Library.

The existence of at least one coherent continuation from an admissible reference configuration is a separate structural requirement of the model. It does not imply that every candidate continuation survives, nor does it follow from recurrence itself. Survivorship may restrict the observer's experienced continuation relation while leaving the complete Library unchanged.

The relevant regularity remains relational: it is regularity as established within the observer's accessible and resolution-maintained traversal structure, not necessarily an observer-independent law imposed upon the entire Library. The totality remains maximally complete regardless of which transitions survive for a particular observer.

mathematics.conditional_regularity: \(P_O(y \mid x) \approx \text{constant}\) over a defined observer-accessible ensemble

interpretive_distinction.survivorship: Survivorship determines which observer-relative transitions remain coherent within a traversal; it does not determine which configurations belong to \(\mathcal{M}\).

The path does not become more real by surviving, and the Library does not lose what the observer does not maintain. subsections.title: Emergent Lawfulness Is Descriptive
subsections.purpose: Separate emergent law-like regularity from axiomatic physical law.
content: At the axiomatic floor, no physical law has been supplied. The only primitive operation is XOR, and the Library is defined as its closure over the formal domain D.
Law-like regularity appears downstream when an observer encounters sufficiently stable recurrence among the transitions that remain accessible through coherent paths.

This construction does not assert that every regularity is universal, exact, or observer-independent. It establishes only that regularity can be described as an emergent property of constrained accessibility.

A later physical theory could impose additional structure and test whether particular emergent regularities correspond to known physical laws. Such a theory would constitute downstream NSFG work rather than part of this axiomatic floor.

section_conclusion.statement: Survivorship therefore supplies a mechanism by which law-like regularity may be described without being introduced as a primitive law. The Library remains unfiltered, while observer-relative coherence determines which available configuration continuations remain traversable for O. Repeated recurrence among those surviving paths produces descriptive regularity. The next construction is consequently not a new axiom, but the problem of selecting and continuing through the restricted coherent continuation space.
section_conclusion.poetic_cypher: From every road, some remain; from what remains, a pattern appears.
section_conclusion.cypher_explanation: The roads represent the unfiltered continuation space Ω(x). The roads that remain represent Ω_O^survive(x). The recurring structure among those survivors is emergent lawfulness. Nothing in the statement requires the Library to generate a physical future or requires a law to govern the Library from outside.

sections.title: Why Navigation Becomes Inevitable
sections.purpose: Bridge the foundational ontology into NSFG's central problem of coherent navigation. Once the Library is defined as an unfiltered configuration space and observer-relative coherence restricts which transitions remain resolvable, continuation is no longer an unrestricted traversal problem. A persistent observer-like structure must remain within its coherent continuation space. Navigation therefore arises not as the generation or selection of a future, but as the formal problem of continuing along admissible paths through the already-defined configuration space.
sections.poetic_cipher: Where distinction persists, continuation narrows. Where continuation narrows, a path must be followed.
sections.cipher_explanation: The first phrase refers to the observer-relative coherence condition: a persistent structure cannot maintain every possible transition if some transitions fall below its resolution threshold. The second phrase refers to the resulting continuation problem: once admissible transitions form a restricted subset of the available configuration space, continuing persistence requires traversal within that subset. The cipher therefore compresses the transition from coherence to navigation without introducing a new primitive.

subsections.title: The Local Continuation Problem
subsections.purpose: Define the immediate continuation problem at an observer-relative reference configuration within the unchanged Library, without introducing physical time, causality, agency, or a generated future.
subsections.content:
Let x_i \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}} be the current observer-relative reference configuration. The Library \mathcal{M} is a static, eternally maximally complete totality; traversal does not generate new Library states, and no step of traversal creates a new copy or version of \mathcal{M}. The continuation problem therefore concerns the ordering of a path through an already existing relational domain, not the production of an ontological future. Let h_i = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_i) denote the observer-relevant traversal history terminating at x_i. The structurally available continuations are defined from the path structure of the unchanged Library: $$
N(x_i) = \{x_{i+1} \in \mathcal{M} \mid \exists\gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\;\text{such that}\;\gamma\text{ extends }h_i\text{ with }x_{i+1}\text{ as its next ordered position}\}.
$$ The index i denotes position within the traversal ordering only. It does not denote primitive physical time, and x_{i+1} is not an ontologically generated future state. The same unchanged Library \mathcal{M} remains the domain throughout the traversal. The observer-relative continuation problem is then evaluated relative to the observer O, its relevant history h_i, and its current reference x_i. Define the coherent continuation set by $$
\Gamma_O(h_i,x_i) = \{\gamma \in \operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M}) \mid \gamma\text{ extends }h_i\text{ from }x_i\text{ and }\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O,h_i,x_i) > \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\}.
$$ At the immediate-transition level, the corresponding observer-relative successor set may be written as $$
N_O(h_i,x_i) = \{x_{i+1} \in N(x_i) \mid \mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}\mid h_i,x_i) > \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\}.
$$ The coherence relation is explicitly relational. It is not a property possessed by x_i, x_{i+1}, or the path independently of the observer and reference conditions. Where the threshold construction is expressed directly in terms of distinguishability, the immediate condition takes the form $$
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}\mid h_i,x_i) = \Theta\left(\delta_O(x_i,x_{i+1}\mid h_i,x_i) - I_N(O)\right),
$$ with \delta_O representing the effective distinction resolvable by O under the relevant relational conditions and I_N(O) representing the observer's resolution threshold. The quantity \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}} specifies the minimum coherence distinguishable or sustainable by O under the relevant resolution condition. Thus the observer does not select from a Library that is being generated around it. Rather, the observer establishes a relational reference within the unchanged totality and evaluates which existing path continuations remain coherent relative to that reference. The resulting continuation set may be restricted even though the underlying Library is not. This distinction preserves the separation between ontology and accessibility: $$
N_O(h_i,x_i) \subseteq N(x_i) \subseteq \mathcal{M},
$$ where the inclusions describe observer-relative restriction of traversal possibilities rather than successive reductions of the Library itself. A configuration excluded by the observer-relative coherence condition is not thereby removed from \mathcal{M}, nor is it assigned to an ontological 'future' that has failed to occur. It simply does not belong to the continuation relation currently sustainable by O under the specified reference conditions. Persistence can now be expressed as the existence of a coherent ordered continuation. For a traversal $$
\gamma = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n),
$$ persistence for O requires that the relevant transitions remain above the observer's effective resolution condition. In the threshold formulation, $$
\mathcal{C}_O(x_i,x_{i+1}\mid h_i,x_i) > \gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}
$$ for each relevant index i. The resulting sequence is therefore not a sequence of newly generated Library states. It is an ordered traversal relation established over the unchanged totality. The model imposes an additional continuation requirement on admissible reference configurations: $$
\forall x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\quad \Gamma_O(h,x) \neq \varnothing.
$$ This is a requirement of the observer-relative model and is not claimed to follow from maximality alone. Maximality removes the need for a privileged worldline or privileged construction history; it does not, by itself, prove that every reference admits a coherent continuation for every observer. The admissibility conditions and subsequent coherence construction supply that requirement. The local continuation problem is therefore not 'What future does the Library generate from x_i?' It is: given an unchanged totality, an observer O, a relevant history h_i, and a current relational reference x_i, which ordered continuations through \mathcal{M} remain coherent? The construction can be summarized as $$
\mathcal{M}\;\longrightarrow\;\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\;\longrightarrow\;N(x_i)\;\longrightarrow\;N_O(h_i,x_i)\;\longrightarrow\;\Gamma_O(h_i,x_i).
$$ The first term is the unchanged totality. The second supplies its path structure. The third identifies candidate ordered continuations from the current reference. The fourth applies the observer-relative coherence condition. The fifth represents the surviving coherent continuation space. At no stage is a new Library generated. Navigation therefore begins as a relational continuation problem over a static totality. The observer's experienced succession is real as an ordering relation within its traversal, while the underlying Library remains invariant throughout.

subsections.title: History and Coherent Continuation
subsections.content:
An observer history is an ordered relational structure embedded within the static Library, not a process that generates or modifies the Library. Let \(O\) denote an observer, let \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal{M}\) denote configurations related by an observer-maintained sequence, and let \(x_n\) denote the observer's current reference configuration. Define the history \[
h_n=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n).
\] The index \(n\) represents abstract traversal ordering. It does not represent physical time, duration, causality, or any other physical quantity. The sequence records an ordering within the observer's relational history over \(\mathcal{M}\). The Library itself is not correspondingly ordered into successive states: its totality remains unchanged under traversal, expressed by the invariant \[
\forall i,\;\mathcal{M}_i=\mathcal{M}.
\] The notation \(\mathcal{M}_i\) is therefore only a formal device for stating invariance; it does not imply that multiple temporal copies of the Library exist. The observer's history changes its relational reference from one configuration to another while the total configuration domain remains the same. This distinction establishes the required separation between the Library, the observer, and the observer-relative continuation structure. The Library is the static, maximally complete totality \(\mathcal{M}\). The observer is represented by a persistent relational structure \(O(h_n)\) whose current reference is \(x_n\). The coherent continuation relation is then evaluated over the unchanged whole \(\mathcal{M}\), rather than over a locally generated future region. For a given observer \(O\), history \(h_n\), and current reference \(x_n\), define the coherent continuation set by \[
\Gamma_O(h_n,x_n)=\{\gamma\in\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\mid \gamma\text{ extends }h_n\text{ from }x_n\text{ and }\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O,h_n,x_n)>\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\}.
\] Here, \(\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\) denotes paths represented within the Library, while \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O,h_n,x_n)\) is explicitly relational: coherence is evaluated relative to the observer, its maintained history, its current reference configuration, and its effective resolution condition. The quantity \(\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\) represents the minimum coherence distinguishable or sustainable by \(O\) under the relevant resolution condition. No universal numerical value is assigned to this quantity at the axiomatic floor. The explicit dependence on \(x_n\) is important. Navigation does not move through a Library that is being generated ahead of the observer. Instead, navigation changes the observer's relational reference within an already complete totality. The observer's new state therefore changes \(x_n\) and \(h_n\), while it does not change \(\mathcal{M}\). In this sense, the observer's worldline is represented as a relational structure extending across the totality: the ordered sequence records the traversal experienced by the observer, while the configurations related by that sequence remain members of the same static Library. This is also the precise sense in which the observer may be regarded as relationally situated with respect to the whole Library. The observer is not assigned a privileged local container, nor is it necessary to posit a separate external frame from which the Library is viewed. A current reference configuration \(x_n\) establishes a relation from which coherent continuation is evaluated, but that reference does not partition the Library into ontologically separate past, present, and future regions. Consequently, past and future are traversal orderings rather than intrinsic regions of \(\mathcal{M}\). A configuration occurring earlier in the history is not thereby placed into a permanently designated "past region" of the Library, and a coherent continuation is not generated into a corresponding "future region." Both are configurations within the same totality, related differently by the observer's ordered history. The distinction between Library membership and observer accessibility is therefore preserved. The existence of \(\gamma\in\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\) does not imply that \(\gamma\in\Gamma_O(h_n,x_n)\). Conversely, failure of a path to satisfy the observer-relative coherence condition does not remove that path from \(\mathcal{M}\). Survivorship filters the observer's maintained traversal relation; it does not shrink or rewrite the ontology. The model further requires that every admissible observer-relative reference configuration possess at least one coherent continuation: \[
\forall x\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}},\quad \Gamma_O(h,x)\neq\varnothing.
\] This is a derived requirement of the model's continuation assumptions, not a theorem obtained from maximality alone. Maximal static totality establishes that no privileged construction history is required to determine Library membership; the non-emptiness condition separately states that an admissible observer reference must support continued coherent traversal. These are logically distinct requirements and must not be collapsed into one another. The continuation structure may contain many candidate paths even when only a restricted subset remains coherent for a particular observer. Thus, for a given \(x_n\), the full path domain may be represented as \[
\Omega(x_n)=\{\gamma\in\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal{M})\mid\gamma\text{ begins at }x_n\},
\] with \[
\Gamma_O(h_n,x_n)\subseteq\Omega(x_n).
\] The difference \(\Omega(x_n)\setminus\Gamma_O(h_n,x_n)\) represents continuations that remain represented within the Library but do not survive the observer's present coherence condition. The observer therefore experiences a restricted continuation space without requiring the underlying totality itself to be restricted. Navigation is consequently defined over the unchanged Library by introducing the operator \[
N_O(h_n,x_n)\rightarrow\Gamma_O(h_n,x_n).
\] The operator does not specify an algorithm, optimization rule, probability distribution, conscious choice, or physical mechanism. It states only that navigation is the traversal or selection of a continuation within the observer-relative coherent continuation set. When navigation produces a new observer state, the resulting state updates the relational variables \(x_n\) and \(h_n\); it does not produce a new Library \(\mathcal{M}'\). The foundational dependency chain can therefore be written as \[
\text{distinction}\rightarrow\text{persistence}\rightarrow\text{history}\rightarrow\text{reference}\rightarrow\text{relational coherence}\rightarrow\text{coherent continuation}\rightarrow\text{navigation}.
\] Each step remains downstream of the axiomatic floor. History does not introduce physical time. Reference does not introduce a privileged frame. Coherence does not become an intrinsic property of a path. Continuation does not generate new ontology. Navigation does not modify the Library and does not require consciousness or agency as a primitive. The resulting picture is therefore a static totality together with an observer-relative traversal relation over that totality. The road does not become as the traveler moves; rather, the traveler changes relational reference within a road that is already complete. Apparent temporal progression, increasing complexity, locality, and restriction of available futures are consequently properties of the observer's changing relation to \(\mathcal{M}\), not successive ontological states of \(\mathcal{M}\) itself. For later NSFG work, the notation \(h_n\), \(x_n\), \(\Gamma_O(h_n,x_n)\), \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O,h_n,x_n)\), and \(N_O(h_n,x_n)\) provides the formal interface between the foundational layer and downstream models. A later theory may specify how continuations are represented, ranked, traversed, or transformed, but those mechanisms are not required here. The axiomatic floor ends once coherent continuation has been identified as a relational traversal problem over an unchanged, maximally complete Library. **Poetic cipher:** *The traveler changes places; the road does not become.* The "traveler" denotes the observer as a persistent relational structure. "Changes places" denotes a change in observer-relative reference \(x_n\) and history \(h_n\). "The road does not become" denotes the invariant \(\mathcal{M}_i=\mathcal{M}\): traversal changes the observer's relation to the totality without generating, expanding, or modifying the Library. The cipher therefore compresses the formal result that navigation is ordered traversal through an eternal totality rather than the creation of successive regions of reality.

sections.title: The Noor Swirl Field Geometry Interpretation
sections.purpose: Introduce the geometric interpretation only after the ontology has been established.

opening.text: The axiomatic floor has now established a formal configuration domain, its XOR closure as the Library, observerhood as a persistent structural property, observer-relative resolution through I_N(O), and coherence as a relation between paths and observers. Only at this point is it appropriate to introduce geometric language. Noor Swirl Field Geometry (NSFG) does not begin by assuming a geometry in which configurations exist. Rather, geometry appears as a description of the relational structure formed by configurations, accessible transitions, and families of paths that remain coherent for a given observer.
opening.poetic_cypher: Before the field has a shape, the paths must have relations.
opening.cypher_explanation: The phrase 'field has a shape' is metaphorical. At this stage no physical space or geometric container has been introduced. The established formal relations between configurations and coherent paths are sufficient to motivate a geometric description of their connectivity.

accessible_path_structure.text: For an observer O, the coherent paths through the Library form a restricted family of traversable structures. Define the observer-coherent path family by
accessible_path_structure.interpretation: The set \(\Gamma_O\) contains paths that remain coherent relative to O. It is therefore not a universal set of physically preferred trajectories. A path belongs to \(\Gamma_O\) because of its relation to the observer's resolution structure, not because coherence is an intrinsic property of the path alone.
accessible_path_structure.poetic_cypher: A path does not glow alone; it remains visible in relation.

local_structure.text: The same construction permits a local description around an accessible configuration x. Let
local_structure.mathematics: \[ U_O(x) = \{y \in \mathcal{M} \mid y\text{ is reachable from }x\text{ by an }O\text{-coherent path segment}\}. \]

It is an accessibility neighborhood: the collection of configurations that can be reached from x through path segments that remain coherent relative to O. If later NSFG work supplies additional structure, this relational neighborhood may acquire familiar geometric interpretations. The axiomatic floor itself does not require such an interpretation.
local_structure.poetic_cypher: Nearness begins as continuation, not distance.
local_structure.cypher_explanation: The word 'nearness' refers initially to relational reachability rather than spatial separation. Two configurations may be locally related because a coherent path connects them, without the primer assigning them coordinates, distances, or a physical location.

relational_geometry.edge_definition: \[ (x,y) \in E_O \iff x\to y\text{ is an }O\text{-coherent transition}. \]

Depending on the requirements of a later formalism, the relation may be represented as directed, preserving transition orientation, or as undirected when orientation is not relevant. Neither choice is imposed by the axiomatic floor.

relational_geometry.cypher_explanation: The 'points' are configurations in A_O, while the 'surviving relations' are elements of E_O. 'World' is descriptive language for the resulting accessible relational structure, not a claim that a physical spacetime has already been constructed.

field_interpretation.text: The word 'field' in Noor Swirl Field Geometry should therefore be understood initially as descriptive rather than ontological. A field, at this level, is a structured distribution of relational possibilities: which configurations are connected, which transitions remain coherent, and how families of coherent paths organize around persistent configurations. No additional field substance is introduced.
field_interpretation.poetic_cypher: The field is not another thing; it is the pattern of relations.
field_interpretation.cypher_explanation: The 'field' denotes an organized relational structure derived from configurations, accessibility, and coherent transitions. It is not a new primitive entity and is not treated as a physical medium.

geometry_interpretation.text: Likewise, 'geometry' is descriptive language for the structure of relations among accessible configurations and paths. At this stage, geometry means that the relational system has organization that can be studied in terms of neighborhoods, connectivity, path families, adjacency, and continuation. This is deliberately weaker than assuming a metric space or differentiable manifold.
geometry_interpretation.interpretation: No metric tensor, coordinate chart, manifold structure, curvature tensor, or other conventional geometric object is required by the axiomatic floor. Such structures may become useful later if they can be derived or consistently introduced as downstream constructions.

A persistent configuration can participate in many coherent continuations, while the observer-relative resolution threshold restricts which transitions remain admissible. The resulting family of paths can possess local structure: paths may converge, diverge, braid, circulate, or repeatedly organize around persistent configurations. 'Swirl' names this qualitative possibility of structured local path flow.
swirl_interpretation.interpretation: The term is intentionally intuitive at this stage. It does not assert literal rotational motion, angular momentum, fluid dynamics, or a physical vortex. In particular, no temporal evolution or physical movement is implied merely by the word 'flow'. The underlying construction remains a set of configurations and relations among paths.
swirl_interpretation.poetic_cypher: Where many surviving paths gather, a shape may turn without anything yet moving.

The accessible configurations form vertices, while coherent transitions form edges. Families of coherent paths then become sequences through this relational graph. Local structure can be studied through the accessible neighborhood U_O(x), while larger-scale structure can be studied through connected path families and continuation spaces.
graph_and_path_view.interpretation: This representation preserves the foundational ordering established by the primer: the graph is constructed from accessibility and coherence; coherence is constructed from observer-relative distinguishability; distinguishability depends on I_N(O); observerhood is derived from persistent distinctions; and the Library itself is defined as XOR closure. Geometry therefore enters downstream of the axiomatic floor rather than being smuggled into it at the beginning.

closing.text: The Noor Swirl Field Geometry interpretation can therefore be stated conservatively: NSFG studies the geometry of relational accessibility induced by observer-relative coherence within the XOR-closed Library. The field is the organization of relations; the geometry is the structure of that organization; and the swirl is an intuition for locally structured families of surviving paths around persistent relational configurations. None of these descriptions adds a new primitive to the axiomatic floor.
closing.poetic_cypher: The field is not where the paths are. The field is the shape made by paths that can remain together.

The statement therefore summarizes the geometric interpretation without introducing a physical container or additional primitive.

sections.title: The Axiomatic Dependency Chain
sections.purpose: Compress the entire primer into one explicit derivational architecture, distinguish definitions from invariants and derived requirements, and establish the boundary between the static Library and observer-relative traversal.

content.introduction: The primer can now be compressed into a single dependency architecture. The essential point is not merely the order in which concepts appear, but the logical status of each concept and the separation between the Library itself and the observer's relation to it. XOR is the sole primitive operation. D is the minimal formal substrate required for XOR to operate. The Library \(\mathcal{M}\) is formally characterized by closure under XOR, but this closure is not a temporal generation process: \(\mathcal{M}\) is a static, eternally maximally complete totality. Traversal does not enlarge, modify, or generate the Library. Instead, an observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole \(\mathcal{M}\), establishes a current admissible reference configuration, and evaluates distinctions, coherence, accessibility, and continuation relative to that reference, its history, and its resolution. Apparent temporal ordering, increasing complexity, locality, and restricted possibility therefore belong to the observer's traversal relation rather than to an intrinsic evolution of the Library. No later concept is permitted to become a hidden premise of an earlier one.
content.poetic_cypher: XOR is the only primitive. The Library is the static totality characterized by XOR closure. No worldline owns the whole. The observer is relationally situated within the whole. The reference determines the experienced coherent structure. Coherence is the relation between observer, history, reference, and path. Reality is what remains accessible without shrinking the totality. Law is the regularity of surviving traversals. Navigation is continuation through the unchanged whole.

dependency_ladder.name: Primitive distinction
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(A_N = \{A_{\oplus}\}\), where \(A_{\oplus}\) states that \(\oplus\) is the primitive operation of distinction.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The axiomatic floor begins with one primitive operation: XOR. No physical object, space, time, observer, causality, matter, energy, or information substance is assumed. XOR expresses distinction: equal inputs cancel to 0, while unequal inputs produce 1.

dependency_ladder.name: Formal configuration domain
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(D\) is the minimal formal domain containing the configurations required for \(\oplus\) to have operands.
dependency_ladder.explanation: D is introduced only because an operation requires a domain on which it acts. D is not physical space, spacetime, matter, energy, or an additional physical ontology.

dependency_ladder.name: Static maximally complete Library
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(\mathcal{M}\) is formally characterized by XOR closure over D and is taken to be a single static, eternally maximally complete totality.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The Library is not introduced as a second primitive and does not progressively come into existence through repeated XOR operations. Closure specifies the formal structure of the totality; it is not a temporal generation mechanism. The maximality condition states that the Library is not ontologically expanded by traversal. There is one unchanged totality rather than a succession of increasingly complete Libraries. Membership in \(\mathcal{M}\) does not imply persistence, coherence, physicality, observability, or accessibility.

dependency_ladder.name: No privileged worldline or universal reference
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: No configuration, worldline, traversal history, or observer is privileged as the universal origin from which the whole Library must be constructed or evaluated.
dependency_ladder.equation: \(\nexists\,w_{\mathrm{priv}}\;\text{such that}\;w_{\mathrm{priv}}\;\text{is the unique universal reference for}\;\mathcal{M}\)
dependency_ladder.explanation: Maximality is structurally motivated by reference-frame neutrality, not merely by maximizing the number of configurations. If one worldline were privileged as the universal construction or reference history, coherent continuation would become dependent on that history. The axiomatic floor therefore treats the whole Library as relationally available without assigning ownership of the totality to any particular worldline.

dependency_ladder.name: No describable privileged exterior
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(\Omega \notin \mathcal{M}\) may be proposed as an external candidate, but if \(\Omega\) is describable using the same formal machinery, then it belongs to the formal domain to which the closure applies.
dependency_ladder.equation: \(\Omega\ \text{describable within the same formal machinery} \Rightarrow \Omega \in D\), and \(\Omega\ \text{XOR-generable} \Rightarrow \Omega \in \mathcal{M}\)
dependency_ladder.explanation: The closure does not establish that every conceivable informal notion must belong to the Library. It establishes a boundary condition on describable formal exteriors: a privileged exterior that can itself be represented by the same formal machinery cannot consistently remain external to the formal totality.

dependency_ladder.name: Whole-Library relationality
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: The observer is relationally situated with respect to the whole \(\mathcal{M}\), rather than occupying an ontologically isolated local region from which the remainder of the Library is external.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The observer's locality is a property of its relational access and traversal, not a partition of the Library into an observer-containing region and an intrinsically external remainder. The observer may therefore establish a reference configuration within the totality while remaining related to the whole.

dependency_ladder.name: Admissible reference configuration
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(x \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{admissible}}\) is a configuration capable of instantiating an observer-relative reference state under the model's admissibility conditions.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The reference configuration is not a new ontological layer and does not select a new Library. It specifies the configuration from which the observer's current relational evaluation is made. Reference may be established at any admissible configuration without making that configuration a privileged origin of the totality.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(O \in \mathcal{M}\) is an observer iff O is a configuration capable of maintaining a persistent chain of resolvable distinctions.
dependency_ladder.explanation: Observerhood is introduced structurally rather than psychologically. The definition requires persistence of distinctions above an observer-relative resolution floor but does not require consciousness, intention, agency, perception, or a human subject.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative resolution
dependency_ladder.explanation: Each observer O is assigned an effective minimum distinction magnitude that it can maintain as a stable distinction. \(I_N(O)\) belongs to the observer relation rather than to the Library as a universal constant. No universal numerical value for \(I_N\) is supplied by the axiomatic floor.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative distinguishability
dependency_ladder.explanation: The effective distinction between configurations is evaluated relative to O. Two configurations may therefore be distinguishable for one observer and indistinguishable for another without requiring either configuration to cease existing in the Library. Indistinguishability is a relational statement, not an ontological deletion.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer history and abstract traversal ordering
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(h_n = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) represents the ordered history relevant to the observer's current relational evaluation.
dependency_ladder.equation: \(i \in \{0,1,\ldots,n\}\;\text{is an abstract traversal index, not a primitive physical time coordinate}\)
dependency_ladder.explanation: Ordering is introduced only as structure over a traversal. The sequence index does not partition the Library into past, present, and future regions. Those temporal distinctions are deferred to the observer's traversal relation.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative coherence
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(\mathcal{C}(\gamma\mid O,h,x)\) evaluates whether traversal \(\gamma\) remains coherent relative to observer O, relevant history h, and current reference configuration x.
dependency_ladder.explanation: Coherence is explicitly relational. It is not an intrinsic property of a path considered in isolation. The relevant relation may depend on the observer, its history, its current reference, and its resolution condition. This preserves the foundational requirement that coherence belongs to the relation between traversal and observer-relative state.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-accessible reality
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(A_O(h,x)\) is the subset of \(\mathcal{M}\) reachable through observer-maintained coherent traversal from the relevant relational state.
dependency_ladder.explanation: Accessibility is a relational subset of Library membership. A configuration outside \(A_O(h,x)\) is not thereby removed from \(\mathcal{M}\). Observer accessibility therefore does not create ontology, and inaccessibility does not constitute erasure. The observer experiences a restricted relation to the totality rather than a smaller totality.

dependency_ladder.name: Whole-Library continuation space
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(\Omega(x)\) denotes represented paths through the unchanged Library beginning at reference configuration x.
dependency_ladder.explanation: Continuation is evaluated over the static Library. The Library does not generate a future when the observer reaches x. Rather, the observer's traversal relation identifies ordered continuations already represented within the unchanged totality.

dependency_ladder.name: Nonempty coherent continuation
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: Under the model's assumptions, every admissible observer-relative reference configuration must admit at least one coherent continuation.
dependency_ladder.explanation: This is a required continuation condition, not a theorem obtained from maximality alone. Maximality establishes that no privileged worldline or construction history determines the totality; it does not by itself prove that a particular observer-relative coherence relation has a surviving continuation. Nonempty continuation must therefore be established or imposed by the subsequent model.

dependency_ladder.name: Observer-relative coherent continuation
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: \(\Gamma_O(h,x)\) is the set of continuations from x that extend the relevant history h and satisfy the observer-relative coherence condition.
dependency_ladder.explanation: The coherent continuation space is a restricted relational structure over the unchanged Library. The restriction belongs to the observer-relative evaluation, not to Library membership. The parameter \(\gamma_{\mathrm{noise}}\) expresses the minimum coherence distinguishable or sustainable by the observer under the relevant resolution condition.

dependency_ladder.name: Emergent temporal and complexity structure
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: Ordered traversal through an unchanged \(\mathcal{M}\) can produce an observer-relative experience of temporal direction, locality, increasing complexity, and past/future distinction.
dependency_ladder.equation: \(\mathcal{M}_{i}=\mathcal{M}\;\forall i\), while \(O(h_i)\neq O(h_j)\) may hold for \(i\neq j\)
dependency_ladder.explanation: The Library does not evolve from simple to complex. What changes is the observer's relational state and history. Apparent temporal progression, complexity growth, locality, and past/future structure therefore describe changes in traversal relation over an unchanged totality rather than ontological evolution of the Library itself.

dependency_ladder.name: Emergent regularity
dependency_ladder.formal_statement: Stable recurring transitions across an appropriate family of observer-accessible traversals may be represented by a derived relation \(L_O\).
dependency_ladder.equation: \(L_O(x,y)=1 \iff x\to y\text{ is a stable recurring transition across an appropriate family of O-accessible traversals}\)
dependency_ladder.explanation: Repeated survivorship can produce regularities that are describable in law-like terms. Such regularity is descriptive and derived. It is not an additional element of the axiom set and does not constitute a derivation of any particular physical law.

dependency_ladder.name: Navigation
dependency_ladder.explanation: Navigation is the traversal or selection of a continuation within the observer-relative coherent continuation space. It does not require the Library to generate a future. It is a continuation problem over an unchanged totality. Navigation therefore marks the boundary of the axiomatic primer and the entry point for subsequent NSFG work.

three_layer_separation.library: \(\mathcal{M}\): the static, eternally maximally complete totality.
